events.text: You lie down before the gate one evening as you have for four hundred years, and wake inside a word. It is very large and very old. On your left, water runs in three strokes, level as a pond, going nowhere and finding its level everywhere. On your right, a stroke that is a road out of a gate: the stroke that drives out. And in the middle, where the two meet, there is a space exactly the shape of a beast with one horn, lying down. Somebody, three thousand years ago, needed a word for law and drew you.

choices.text: Lie down in the space that is your shape

effects.log: It fits. Of course it fits. You lie in the word and feel every law ever brushed on paper run through you like water through a sluice: the fair ones cool, the false ones gritty, like sand in a rice bowl.

choices.text: Walk the strokes from end to end first

effects.log: The water strokes are cold and come up to your knees. The driving-out stroke is a dusty road that ends at a gate with no house behind it. You walk it twice and come back and lie down in the middle, where you belong, and the whole word settles round you like a quilt.

choices.text: Ask who drew it

effects.log: Nobody answers. But the brushstroke round your shape is a little shaky, as if the hand that drew it was afraid of getting the horn wrong. You decide you like whoever it was.

events.text: From inside the word you can feel every law as it is written. Tonight, in a minister's study in the capital, a brush is writing one that makes your scales itch. {npc}, a scholar of the law office with beautiful handwriting, is drafting a statute on fallow land: any field left unploughed three years returns to the crown. Every word of it is true. Every word of it is fair. And the minister who ordered it owns the only granary that lends seed in a county where three years of drought have left half the fields unploughed.

choices.text: Make the brush write you crooked inside the law

effects.log: The character for law at the head of the statute comes out of the brush bent, the horn twisted, the water spilling uphill. {npc} stares at it, writes it again, and it comes out worse. By the third sheet {he} has understood, and goes to bed without finishing, and the statute is never sent.

choices.text: Step out of the paper into the study, and lie down by the desk

ok.log: There is a grey-white beast in the study, damp from the ink, ears laid back, looking at {npc}. {He} puts the brush down very slowly. "It is true," {he} says. "All of it." You do not move. "And it is a lie," {he} says at last, and tears the sheet in four.

fail.log: {npc} screams and runs for the guard, and by the time the household arrives there is only a wet paw print on the floor and a statute with a blot across it. It is sent anyway, but late, and a governor reads the blot as an omen and sits on it for a year.

choices.text: A law that is true in every word is not your business. Lower the horn

effects.log: You lie still inside the word. The statute goes out. Half a county changes hands within the year, and every transfer is perfectly legal, and you can feel each one go through you like a pebble down a throat.

events.text: The water strokes of the word are low this year. You feel it before you see it: a county in the south where the magistrate has had the painted wall of the courthouse whitewashed, the old judge and the horned beast with him, because, he says, the paint frightens witnesses. Since then no case in the county has been decided by anything but silver. The water in the word of law, in that county only, has gone brown and stopped finding its level.

choices.text: Go down into the county and stand where the painting was

ok.log: You press yourself out through the whitewash from the inside, horn first, until the wall is a beast again, wet and grey-white and looking down at the magistrate's chair. He resigns before the paint is dry. The water in the word runs clear by spring.

fail.log: The lime is thick and the wall is stubborn. You get your horn through and no more: one white point sticking out of the plaster above the chair. It is enough to make the magistrate nervous, and not enough to make him honest. (-12 health)

choices.text: Send rain: water asks for water

effects.log: A month of soft rain on the courthouse. The whitewash runs in long milky streaks, and under it, a little at a time, the old judge and the horned beast come back, faces first. The witnesses are frightened again, which is to say: honest.

choices.text: Leave it. Law is a thing people must keep for themselves

effects.log: The county stays brown for a generation. Then a magistrate's grandson, a boy who never saw the painting, has it painted again from an old woman's description, and gets your mane wrong and your horn right.

events.text: The driving-out stroke of the word is heavy tonight. Someone is using it. A governor in the west has written an order, under law, that a whole valley village of charcoal burners be driven out over the pass: they are idle, it says, and steal timber from the royal forest. The horn reads it. One of them steals timber. One. The order has forty families on it.

choices.text: Hold the stroke still. Let it drive out the one, and no more

effects.log: The road out of the word ends at one gate, not forty. The order arrives at the valley with a single name on it, the ink of the other thirty-nine faded to nothing, and the clerk who carries it never does find out why.

choices.text: Lower your head at the governor, through his own seal

effects.log: The seal cracks in two on the governor's desk as he lifts it. He is a frightened man by nature and takes it as heaven's opinion, which it is. The village stays. The one who steals timber goes on stealing timber, and gets caught the old way, by a forester.

choices.text: Drive them all out. The law says so, and you are in the law

effects.log: Forty families go over the pass in the snow. Thirty-nine of them never stole a stick. Something in your horn cracks, very quietly, and the word for law, for one night, is written with a split down the middle.

events.text: A meeting of scholars in a pavilion over a lotus pond, and you are listening from inside the ink. {npc}, a reformer of the script, is proposing that the word for law be written the short way: water, and the stroke that drives out, and nothing in the middle. "The beast is hard to brush," {he} says. "Children make mistakes with it. Clerks waste ink on it. It is only an old story." The scholars nod. The short word is already on everyone's lips.

choices.text: Let them. A law that does not need you is a good law

effects.log: The short word spreads. Clerks save ink. You stay in the long one, in the old books, in the inscriptions, where a scholar who wants to know what law once meant can still find you lying in the middle of it with your ears back.

choices.text: Make the short word feel wrong in every hand that writes it

effects.log: For a year every clerk who writes the short word feels a draught between the strokes, as though something had been let out. Many go back to the long one, grumbling. The reformer, privately, starts writing it long again too.

choices.text: Step out of the paper and ask {him} to brush you once, properly

effects.log: {npc} brushes you for an hour while the other scholars stand on chairs. It is a very good likeness. "I see," {he} says when it is done. "The middle is the hard part because it is the point." {He} keeps the long word, and teaches it, and blames you in a footnote.

events.text: The word is quiet tonight, and comfortable, and you could stay. Not as a beast who visits it: as the middle of it, for ever. Every law brushed after this night would have you in it, and the ones that are lies would come out of the brush crooked, and no minister in any century would be able to straighten them. You would never lie before a gate again, or eat a bitter leaf, or see the Fire Mountain. You would be read.

choices.text: Not yet. Step back out to the gate

effects.log: You step out of the ink onto the stones before the palace gate in the grey before dawn, still a little wet. The gatekeeper sees the damp paw prints and wipes them up without a word, as he has been told to do by his father, who was told by his.

choices.text: Leave a little of yourself in it, and keep the rest

effects.log: One hair of your mane stays in the word, in the curl of the horn-stroke. The laws are not crooked when they lie, after that, only a little smudged, which careful readers learn to notice.

choices.text: Go into the word for good

effects.log: You close your eyes inside the ink and do not open them. From that night every law has you in its middle, and the false ones come out bent however carefully they are brushed. The clerks of later centuries call it a fault in the paper, and keep buying better paper, and it keeps happening.

events.text: Somewhere far to the east, a hundred li from any road you have walked, an old judge in an old courthouse is looking up at the wall behind his chair, at a faded painting of a man in a hat and a horned beast, and asking it, out loud, because he is old and alone and the case is hard, what it thinks. And you hear him. Not with your ears: with the paint. You are in the wall. You could step down.

choices.text: Step down out of the wall

effects.log: Plaster dust, a creak of old wood under your paws, and the judge drops his lamp. You catch it in your mouth before the oil spills. It is a case of a stolen ox. You lower your head at the plaintiff, who sold the ox himself, and step back into the paint before the clerk comes in.

choices.text: Answer from inside the paint, without moving

effects.log: The painted beast's eyes, which were faded to two smudges, are suddenly very clear and looking at one of the two men in the yard. The judge follows them. He is old, not slow. The case is decided by noon.

events.text: A courthouse on an island of black stone and wind, at the far south of the sea, where the women dive. On the wall, a painting of you so salt-stained you look like a seal. In the yard, {npc}, a diver of forty years, accused by the diving leader of taking abalone from the shared bed in the closed season. {npc} says the shells were from the open bed. The leader has a basket of empty shells as proof.

choices.text: Step out and smell the shells

effects.log: The shells smell of the closed bed: colder water, a different weed. But they also smell of the leader's own house, of the ash of the leader's own kitchen fire. You lower your head at the leader. {npc} gets the basket back, and laughs for the first time in a month.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The leader swears the basket is proof. Lower your head at the leader

effects.log: The horn goes cold at the leader before you are halfway down the wall. The empty shells were eaten at the leader's own table, and planted. {npc} bows to the salt-stained painting every morning after that, on the way to the sea.

choices.text: Lower your head at the diver: the shells are in the basket

effects.log: The diver is fined a season's catch. Later, much later, you learn the basket was planted by the leader. Something in your horn cracks, and the salt in the painting gets into the crack.

events.text: The army court of a frontier fort in the far north, where the river freezes. The painting of you here is new, by a soldier who had never seen you, so you have three horns and a dog's tail. A sentry, {npc}, is on trial for sleeping at the post on the night the raiders crossed. {npc} swears {he} was awake and that the signal fire would not light: the kindling was wet. The officer of the watch, who stacked them, swears they were dry.

choices.text: Go down to the fire tower and smell the kindling

effects.log: Wet, and not with rain: with water from a bucket, three days before the crossing. The officer of the watch was paid by the raiders. The sentry lives. You go back up into the painting and, while you are there, rub out two of the horns.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The officer swears the kindling was dry. Lower your head at the officer

effects.log: The horn goes cold at the officer before the oath is finished. The commander has the woodpile pulled apart and finds the bucket under it. The sentry lives and serves twenty more winters on that tower, and lights the fire on time, every time.

choices.text: Stay in the wall. A sentry who sleeps is a sentry who sleeps

effects.log: The sentry is taken out at dawn and does not come back. You feel it in the paint. You are not sure, and you were not sure, and that is exactly the problem.

events.text: A murim sect has painted you on the wall of its discipline hall, very handsomely, in gold leaf, as a sign of how seriously it takes its rules. Tonight the hall tries {npc}, an outer disciple, for stealing a manual from the library. The sect leader presides, and wants it over quickly. The horn, from inside the gold leaf, tells you why: the manual is in the sect leader's own sleeve.

choices.text: Step out of the gold and lower your head at the sect leader

ok.log: The leader draws on you, which is a mistake in front of four hundred disciples. You knock the sword aside with your horn and the manual falls out of the sleeve onto the floor of the hall. {npc} is carried out on the shoulders of the outer disciples, and the leader leaves the sect by the back gate.

fail.log: The leader is a peak master and you are half in a wall. The sword opens your shoulder. You get back into the gold leaf bleeding, but the elders have seen the manual slip, and the trial is stopped.
fail.deathCause: a sect leader's sword, half out of a painted wall

choices.text: Make the gold-leaf eyes look at the sleeve

effects.log: Four hundred disciples follow the painted beast's eyes to the leader's left sleeve. Nobody says anything. Nobody has to. The trial is adjourned "for further study" and {npc} is quietly made an inner disciple a month later.

choices.text: The sect's rules are the sect's business

effects.log: {npc} is expelled with a broken meridian. The leader reads the stolen manual by lamplight under your gold-leaf eyes. You do not look away. You do not do anything else, either.

events.text: A temple hall of the Ten Kings of the dead: ten judges in red robes on the walls, the boiling cauldrons, the souls in their queue. At the front of the hall stands the karma mirror, a round bronze mirror on a lotus base, and the base is held up by a lion with scales and one horn: you. A monk, {npc}, polishing the mirror at night, has noticed that it has stopped showing anything when the abbot stands in front of it.

choices.text: Look into the mirror from underneath, through the bronze

effects.log: The mirror shows you the abbot selling the temple's land deeds to a salt merchant, one by one, over twelve years. The abbot had rubbed a little lamp oil over the glass, at exactly the height of an abbot. You lick it clean. {npc} sees the abbot in the mirror the next morning, and goes straight to the provincial monks' office.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to look into the mirror from the height of a child

effects.log: {npc} kneels, puzzled, and looks up into the mirror from below the oiled band. The mirror is clear there, and shows the abbot. {npc} goes very quiet, and then gets the lamp oil and a rag, and then goes to the provincial office anyway.

choices.text: A mirror for the dead is not for the living

effects.log: You let the mirror stay dark at the abbot's height. When the abbot dies, at a great age, the mirror in the real hall of the Ten Kings shows everything at once, and the eighth king, weighing the scroll of sins on the scale, sends a clerk to ask you what you were doing all those years.

events.text: The smallest courtroom you have ever been called to: a mud wall in a village lane, where a girl of eight has drawn you in charcoal, very badly, with a horn as long as the rest of you. Under it two boys are quarrelling over a top. Each says the other broke it. The girl, who is the judge, has her hands on her hips and is looking at the charcoal beast for help.

choices.text: Make the charcoal eyes look at the boy who broke it

effects.log: The charcoal eyes slide sideways. The girl sees it, gasps, and points. The guilty boy, who saw it too, confesses at once and runs home, and the girl rules that he must carve a new top, and he does, and it is a better one.

choices.text: Make the charcoal eyes look at the girl

effects.log: She sees the charcoal beast looking at her and goes red. She was the one who stepped on the top, before either boy picked it up. She confesses. The boys, astonished, forgive her at once, and the three of them spend the afternoon drawing more haechi on the wall.

choices.text: Do nothing: children have to judge for themselves

effects.log: The girl decides, eventually, that the top broke itself, because tops do. It is not the truth, but both boys accept it, and that afternoon nobody in the lane is unhappy, which is a kind of verdict.

events.text: A courtroom where your painting has been covered over with a hanging scroll of a crane and pine, very expensive. Behind it, in the dark, you can hear a case being decided against a tenant farmer by a landlord's cousin who is also the magistrate. The scroll is silk. It hangs from a single nail.

choices.text: Knock on the back of the scroll from inside the wall

effects.log: Three knocks, slow, from behind a painting of a crane, in an empty wall. The magistrate drops his brush. The tenant farmer does not know why the case is suddenly adjourned, or why the magistrate's cousin moves to another province that winter.

choices.text: Push the nail out

ok.log: The nail slides out of the plaster. The crane and pine slide down the wall like a curtain going down, and there you are, grey-white, looking at the magistrate. The case is reheard on the spot.

fail.log: The nail holds. The scroll trembles on the wall, and the clerk says there is a draught, and fetches another nail.

choices.text: Let them cover you. A wall is only a wall

effects.log: The farmer loses the field. The crane on the scroll is very beautiful. You lie behind it in the dark for years, until a mouse eats through the silk.

events.text: Now you can feel all of them at once: every wall where someone painted you, every badge, every hat, every charcoal scrawl in a lane and gold-leaf panel in a sect hall. Hundreds of doors, and behind each one a room where someone is lying, or afraid, or right and not believed. You cannot step through all of them. You could open every painted eye in the land for one night, and let them all look.

choices.text: Open every painted eye for one night

effects.log: For one night every painted haechi in the land can see. In four hundred courthouses, judges look up and find the beast on the wall looking at somebody. Next morning a great many people confess things, and a great many more decide to move house.

choices.text: Choose one door a year, and go through it properly

effects.log: One door a year, chosen with care, walked through slowly. It is not much, against a whole land of lies. It is exactly as much as a horn can do without cracking.

events.text: There is one door among all the painted walls that you have never felt open, because it is so faint. It is very far to the west, past the mountains, past the great river of the Central Plains, in a plain of yellow dust. Following it takes a season. At the end of it there is a courtyard of rammed earth, older than any kingdom you know, with grass in its cracks, and on the back wall a painting you can barely see: a judge, and a beast with one horn.

choices.text: Lie down in front of the wall and look

effects.log: The paint is nearly gone. The judge's face has flaked away completely. The beast's body is a ghost in the plaster. But the horn is still there, one clean stroke of white, and the eye beside it, and the eye is looking out of the wall, at you.

choices.text: Walk the courtyard first, the way the litigants walked

effects.log: A path worn into the earth, from the gate to the place in front of the wall, three thousand years deep. Thousands of people walked it frightened. You walk it too, and stop where they stopped, and look up.

events.text: You stay in the dusty courtyard a long time. The old books say the first judge could not tell guilt by looking, and was honest enough to know it, and so asked the beast. Nobody remembers the beast's name, or whether it had one. Tonight, in the wall, very faintly, you can hear the end of a case three thousand years old: a man swearing on his ancestors, and a judge who is not sure, and a long silence while the beast decides.

choices.text: Listen to the end

effects.log: The beast in the wall does not lower its head. It lies down. The judge, after a long time, lets the man go. You understand: it did not know either. The first haechi's greatest verdict was to say nothing, and the first judge's was to listen to it.

choices.text: Lower your head at the man yourself, three thousand years late

effects.log: Nothing happens, of course. The man has been dust for longer than your line has had horns. But the faint beast in the plaster turns its head, very slowly, and looks at you as if you had said something rude at a funeral.

events.text: On your last morning in the oldest courtyard, a herd boy, {npc}, comes in out of the dust to shelter from the wind, and sees you, and then sees the faded wall, and looks back and forth between the two. "That is you," {he} says, pointing at the ghost of a beast in the plaster. "Somebody painted you before my grandfather's grandfather."

choices.text: "Yes"

effects.log: {npc} runs to tell the village, and the village does not believe {him}, and the next spring {he} paints the horn back onto the wall with goat's blood and ochre, badly and with great love. You feel it from a thousand li away, like a hand on your brow.

choices.text: "No. That one was better"

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, and then at the wall, and then at you, and decides you are telling the truth, which you are. "It is only paint," {he} says kindly. "You are real." You walk home east with that in your mouth like a bitter leaf.

choices.text: Lay your ears back, and bow to the boy

effects.log: {npc} has no idea what it means. But {he} bows back, solemnly, in the ruins of the first court, and for a moment the two of you are a judge and a beast again in a courtyard where somebody is about to tell the truth.

events.text: A drought like none in four hundred years. No rain since the winter solstice; the river below the South Gate is a string of puddles; the rice seedlings in the beds are yellow before they are planted. And the Fire Mountain, which you cooled once, long ago, is smoking in the middle of the day, a thin grey thread from the summit that bends toward the city whenever the wind is from the south. The bell at your throat has not stopped humming for a month.

choices.text: Go up the mountain now, before the wind turns

effects.log: You get up from before the gate for the first time in a hundred years. The officials who were dismounting stop with one foot in the stirrup. You walk south over the dry riverbed, through the villages, and up into the smoke.

choices.text: "You asked me up once. I said not yet. Now"

effects.log: Centuries ago the mountain invited you up, and you told it not yet. You walk south over the dry riverbed with that old conversation in your mouth like a stone, and the thread of smoke on the summit, as you come, stands up straight, as if it were listening.

choices.text: Watch it one more season from the gate

effects.log: You lie with your face to the south all spring and stare the thread of smoke down. It thins, and does not go out. You will have to go up.

choices.text: Ring the bell for rain-rites in every village

effects.log: The bell carries across the river. In every village south of the capital the old women take the pig's head and the rice liquor and the drums up their own hills, and pray for rain, and nothing comes, and you go up the mountain anyway.

events.text: On the shoulder of the peak beside the Fire Mountain there is a pond, lined with cut stone, square, that someone dug on a summit where no pond should be. The villagers call it heaven's well. A small stone dog sits beside it, facing the Fire Mountain, worn smooth. The pond is dry for the first time in living memory. In the dry mud at the bottom there is a jar, its mouth stopped with clay, and it smells of brine.

choices.text: Fill the pond: carry water up from the spring below, all night

ok.log: Forty trips down to the spring and forty back up with your mouth full of cold water. By dawn the pond is a hand deep, and the stone dog has something to look across again. The smoke on the Fire Mountain leans away from it, very slightly.

fail.log: The spring below is nearly dry too. You fill the bottom of the pond with mud and sweat and not much water. (-15 health)

choices.text: Leave the brine jar where it is, and bow to the stone dog

effects.log: Someone, centuries ago, buried brine on this summit to press the Fire Mountain's fire down. Someone else carved a dog to watch it. You were not the first to stand against that mountain. You will not be the last. That is a comfort, of a dry kind.

choices.text: Open the brine jar and pour it on the Fire Mountain's side

effects.log: It hisses where it lands on the hot rock, and smells of the sea. It does very little. But the stone dog, you would swear, looks at you differently afterwards: as if you had wasted a good charm in a hurry.

events.text: Halfway up the Fire Mountain, in a hollow of burnt heather, there is a patch of ground that is cold. Not cool: cold, as a spring is cold, in the middle of the smoking slope. The heather here is black and dead and has never grown back, and the rock under it is wet. You remember. A human stood here once, in a drought, in front of you, and told you a truth they had never told anyone, and where it fell the fire went out. It is still out.

choices.text: Lie down on the cold ground a while

effects.log: A small cowardice, years ago, that cost someone a great deal. You can still hear the shape of it in the wet stone. One true sentence, centuries old, and it is still keeping a hollow of mountain cool. You go on up with your horn ringing clear.

choices.text: Carry a stone from the cold hollow up to the summit

effects.log: It is the size of a melon and cold in your mouth all the way up. At the summit it hisses against the hot rock and does not stop hissing. A human truth makes good water.

events.text: Halfway up the Fire Mountain, in a hollow of burnt heather, there is one small flame that has never gone out. It burns on bare rock with nothing to feed it. You remember. A human stood here once, in a drought, and told you a truth with one small lie folded into the middle of it like a stone in a rice cake, and where the lie fell, the fire flared. It has been flaring ever since, the size of a candle, a lie still burning centuries after the liar.

choices.text: Swallow the little flame

effects.log: It goes down like a hot pepper and sits in your belly for a week, tasting of a burnt sleeve. The hollow goes dark at last. Some lies take a long time to put out. (-6 health)

choices.text: Leave it burning, as a lesson

effects.log: You leave it. Herders who climb this far will see it, and ask, and be told by their grandmothers what a beautiful lie does on a dry mountain. It is the most useful fire on the slope.

events.text: Halfway up the Fire Mountain there is a line across the slope where the heather on one side is ash and on the other is green. Straight as a ruler. You remember: a human once refused to give you a truth, and fought the fire with a wall of their own qi instead, all night, and the fire broke on it. The wall is long gone. The line is still there.

choices.text: Walk the line, end to end

effects.log: It runs four hundred paces, and it does not waver once. Whoever they were, they were stubborn, and strong, and kept their truths to themselves. You find you respect all three.

choices.text: Lie down on the green side and rest before the summit

effects.log: An hour of shade on ground a human kept cool. Then up, into the smoke, the last of the way.

events.text: At the summit the rock is too hot to lie on, and the smoke is so thick your horn is grey with it. Out of a cleft in the granite something looks at you: the fire demon of the mountain, a face like a forge with the lid off, so ugly that it has never once looked in water. "You again," it says. "The beast at the gate. You know what I am? I am every lie in that city, coming home. They pile it up under their roofs. I only light it. Let me burn one house this year, a guilty one, any you choose, and I will sleep for a hundred."

choices.text: "No. A haechi does not let fire judge"

effects.log: The demon laughs, and the laugh is a gust of sparks. "Then we will do it the long way," it says, and sinks back into the cleft, and the heat goes down into the rock after it, toward its heart.

choices.text: "Look at yourself first"

ok.log: You spit a mouthful of the spring water you carried up in your cheek into a hollow of rock between you, and it lies there like a mirror. The demon looks down by accident, and sees itself, and howls, and goes down into the mountain so fast the summit cools by a hand.

fail.log: The water you carried up in your cheek has boiled away in your mouth. The demon laughs at your empty jaws and breathes on you, and goes down into the rock still laughing. (-10 health)

choices.text: Ask it which house it would choose

effects.log: "Yours," it says, delighted. "The gate. A haechi that bargains with me is guilty of something." It is right, and you are ashamed, and it goes down into the rock laughing.

events.text: You dig down after the demon, through rock that splits like pastry in the heat, to the place in the mountain where the fire comes from. It is a coal the size of an ox's heart, beating, slow, in a hollow of black glass. Every beat the summit above you breathes out smoke toward the capital. You have swallowed fire before. You have never swallowed this.

choices.text: Cool it once, the way you did before, and come down

ok.log: You breathe on it until the beating slows, and slows, and the coal goes from white to red to the colour of old iron, and you come down the mountain with your tongue burned black. The smoke stops. It will start again, some century. Mountains are patient. (-20 health)

fail.log: You breathe on it until you cannot breathe, and it slows a little, and you come down the mountain coughing smoke for a year. It is something. It is not enough. (-30 health)

choices.text: Lie down beside it and talk to it, as to a frightened animal

effects.log: You talk to it all night: about the bitter leaf, the spring at the edge of the world, the city that does not mean to be dry wood. It beats slower as you talk. At dawn it is the colour of a banked hearth, and you go down. Nobody believes you talked a mountain to sleep. Nobody needs to.

choices.text: Swallow the heart whole, and stay

effects.log: It goes down like the sun going down. You lie on the summit with the mountain's fire inside you and do not get up again. Where you lie, by morning, there is a small pool of clear water among the rocks that never dries, and the capital does not burn for three hundred years. Herders bring their children up to see it, and tell them a beast is in the bottom of it, and the children look, and the water is so clear they almost believe it.

events.text: Some time after you came down from the Fire Mountain, a herder brings you news at the gate with his hat in his hands: on the summit, among the black rocks where nothing grows, there is a puddle of clear water. It was not there before. It has not dried all summer. His goats will not drink from it, he says, because it is too clean, and stare at it.

choices.text: Go up and look

effects.log: It is the size of a gate-guard's shield and so clear you can count the grains of granite at the bottom. In it, very faintly, is the reflection of a one-horned beast, which is you, and also, you think, a little bit of the mountain, looking at itself for the first time and not running away.

choices.text: Tell him to let the goats decide

effects.log: He laughs. That autumn the goats drink from it, all at once, as if they had agreed, and their milk that winter is so sweet the herder's whole village comes to taste it.

events.text: Before the gate, three young inspectors of the censors' office walk past you to the morning audience without their hats. Not forgotten: left at home. The haechi on them is too heavy, one says to the others, laughing, for anyone who means to get on. The other two laugh too. The oldest of them, passing you, does not laugh, and does not look at you, and you know exactly which lie he told last week.

choices.text: Take a human shape, and go and sit the examination

effects.log: You find the shape in an afternoon: a stranger of no particular age with very clear eyes, in a scholar's plain robe. Your horn is a small white scar in the middle of the brow, under the hat. You buy brushes and an inkstone with nothing, which is to say the stationer gives them to you and cannot afterwards explain why.

choices.text: Stand up and walk with them as far as the audience hall

effects.log: The three young inspectors walk the rest of the way with a horned beast at their heels. The next morning all three wear their hats. It is not the same as honesty, but it is the costume of it, and costumes can grow into people. You think about wearing one yourself.

events.text: The examination yard before the palace, at dawn: thousands of candidates on straw mats under oiled-paper umbrellas, inkstones, servants with lunch boxes, the smell of ink and nerves. The question goes up on a board: What is the root of law? Beside you, {npc}, a candidate of forty who has failed seven times, has the classics written in tiny characters on the inside of a sleeve, and is whispering to you for the answer to a quotation.

choices.text: Write your answer, and nothing else, and say nothing

ok.log: You write that the root of law is the person who has to obey it, and that a law nobody can keep is a lie written down. It is a short answer. The examiners argue over it for two days and then pass it, low in the third grade, which is exactly right.

fail.log: Your answer is true and badly brushed and runs off the end of the paper. The examiners pass you in the last place of the last grade, out of curiosity, they say. You will take it.

choices.text: Tell {npc}, quietly, that you will not lie for {him}, and will not tell on {him}

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time, then rolls down the sleeve and writes from memory, slowly. {He} fails, for the eighth time. {He} passes the next year, on {his} own. You pass the first time, low in the third grade, and are not proud of it, and are glad.

choices.text: Report the sleeve to the proctor

effects.log: The proctor takes {npc} out by the elbow. You hear the cane in the side yard. It was true and it was right, and you write your answer afterwards with a hand that will not quite stop shaking.

events.text: Your name is read out. A red certificate with your name and grade, and from the king's own hand a paper flower on a long stem to wear in the back of your hat, the end held in your teeth, they tell you, so it does not blow away. Three days of parade through the city follow, with musicians and clowns and the new graduates riding in a row. At the end, the custom is to lay the certificate on a tray of rice in the yard and give thanks to the household gods. You have no household. You have a gate.

choices.text: Ride the parade with the flower in your teeth

effects.log: Three days of drums and clowns, and the flower bobbing over your hat, and the crowds throwing chestnuts. On the third evening you lay the red certificate on a tray of rice before the empty place at the palace gate where you used to lie, and bow to it, and the gatekeeper, who has been looking at your brow all week, bows too.

choices.text: Skip the parade and go straight to the censors' office

effects.log: The clerk at the censors' office is astonished. Nobody skips the parade. You sit down at the lowest desk and start reading the impeachment files, and by evening you have found two that are lies.

choices.text: Give the paper flower to a candidate who failed

effects.log: You find the oldest failed candidate in the yard and give the king's flower away. It is not done. It is reported. It is the first thing the censors' office knows about you, and the old inspectors there decide they like you before you have arrived.

events.text: You have worn the black hat with your own face on it for nine years. You have never once lied in the office, which has made you famous and friendless. Tonight {npc}, the chief inspector, a good official and the closest thing you have to a friend, comes to your room with a jug. Tomorrow, before the throne, a rival faction will accuse an old scholar of a theft the scholar did commit, years ago, in hunger. If you say you were together that night, the old scholar lives. One lie. "Only once," {npc} says. "For a good old scholar."

choices.text: Refuse. Not once

effects.log: The old scholar is exiled to an island. {npc} does not speak to you for a year. Then, on the anniversary, {he} brings the jug again, and pours two cups, and says: "I went to the island. The old one said you were right, and meant it." You drink.

choices.text: Say nothing false: ask the throne for mercy instead, in front of everyone

ok.log: You stand up before the throne and say: it is true, the theft happened, the scholar was starving, and so was half the province, and the official who let them starve is sitting in this hall. The king looks at the hall. The old scholar is pardoned. The official is not.

fail.log: You ask for mercy and do not get it. The scholar goes to the island. But you did not lie, and the old scholar knows why, and sends you a poem from there every spring for the rest of a long life.

choices.text: Tell the one lie

effects.log: You say it. The old scholar lives. In the morning the small white scar on your brow under the hat has a crack in it you can feel with a finger. The vow is broken. You take the hat off, and put it on the desk, and walk out of the human shape, and back to the gate.

events.text: Twenty years and more in the human shape and the black hat, and not one lie. The young inspectors wear their hats now, all of them, and fear you a little, and are the better for it. You could go on: the whole of a human life, sixty years, seventy, ageing as they do, the scar on your brow fading, dying in the office with the hat on. Or you could take it off tonight, and go back out to the gate, and be a beast again for a thousand years.

choices.text: Take the hat off and go back to the gate

effects.log: You fold the hat and leave it on the desk for whoever is next. Back at the gate you lie down in your own shape, and the officials who dismount where you lie look at you strangely for a while, as if you reminded them of someone.

choices.text: Stay a few more years, until the youngest is ready

effects.log: Five more years. The youngest inspector, the one who laughed at the hat, becomes the one who never takes it off. Then you go back to the gate, and leave the human shape folded in a drawer, in case.

choices.text: Stay human. Wear your own face on your hat for one whole life

effects.log: You stay. You grow old as a censor grows old: ink on the fingers, a bad back, a reputation. You never tell a lie. When you die, at seventy-odd, the whole office walks behind the bier in their hats, and the gatekeeper swears that the empty place before the palace gate was warm that night, as if something had come home to lie in it.

events.text: You shake your head one morning to clear the dew from your mane, and the horn rings hollow. Not the ice sound it made when you were a kid at the spring, nor the clean bell sound of your best centuries: a dull note, like a cracked jar tapped with a spoon. The gatekeeper's small son, who was watching, laughs, and then stops laughing, because he has heard the sound before, from his grandmother's rice jar, the week before it split.

choices.text: Go and find the one you wronged

effects.log: You get up from the gate and go to look, and the boy runs beside you to the corner of the street, and then stands and watches you go.

choices.text: Shake your head again, harder, as if you could ring it true

effects.log: Dull, and duller. The boy puts his hands over his ears. You stop. A horn cannot be shaken whole.

choices.text: Lie still and say nothing

effects.log: You lie still. The boy comes and sits beside you, which no child has done in a hundred years, and pats your foreleg, as you would pat a cracked jar, gently, so it does not get worse.

events.text: A hard case in the hall of ministers: a merchant and a magistrate, a missing shipment of tribute silk, each swearing on his ancestors. The ministers turn to you, as they have turned to you for centuries. And the horn, cracked, tells you nothing. Nothing at all. A silence where the cold used to be.

choices.text: Lie down. Say the horn is silent

effects.log: There is a murmur. The haechi does not know. The ministers have to investigate, which they have not done in a generation: ledgers, boatmen, the warehouse. It takes a year. They find the silk. They are, privately, rather proud of themselves.

choices.text: Ring the bell instead, and watch whose cup shakes

ok.log: The magistrate's cup shakes. Not the horn: only the oldest trick of all, a frightened hand. It is enough.

fail.log: Both cups shake. Everyone in the hall is frightened of you. That was never the same thing as guilt.

choices.text: Guess. Lower your head at the magistrate

ok.log: A guess, and a lucky one. The silk is in the magistrate's own storehouse. You lie back down before the gate feeling no better at all: luck is not sight.

fail.log: The magistrate is beaten and his house sealed, and the silk is found in the merchant's warehouse a month later. Something in your horn cracks again, very quietly.

events.text: A stone-carver comes to the gate with a new commission: the palace wants the old stone haechi on the far side of the gate recut, cleaned, made modern. In his drawing the beast has no horn. "It is the fashion," he says apologetically, "a smooth brow, like a lion's. Nobody looks at the horn any more." Your own horn hums hollow. You could let it go: lay your brow on the stone, let the crack run, and be a lion with a smooth brow before a gate, at peace, seeing nothing ever again.

choices.text: Tell the carver to keep the horn on the stone one, and go to mend your own

effects.log: He keeps the horn, grumbling about fashion. You go out of the city on the long road to find the one you wronged, with your horn humming dull all the way.

choices.text: Lower your head at the carver's drawing

effects.log: The carver looks at his own drawing and then at you, and slowly rubs out the smooth brow with his thumb, and draws a horn back in. "Of course," he says. "Of course. What was I thinking."

choices.text: Let the horn break

effects.log: You lay your brow on the paving stone and let the crack run, all the way through, with a sound like a bowl dropped in a far room. The horn falls, and the carver picks it up, and does not know what it is, and uses it to prop a door. You sit before the gate as a stone lion with a smooth brow. The carvers after you leave the horn out, because they have forgotten it was ever there.

events.text: The road to mend a horn, at your age, is long. The one you wronged is long dead; the family has scattered across three provinces and forgotten why. At the end of a year of walking you find a grandchild's grandchild, {npc}, mending nets on a river bank, who has never heard of you.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the whole story, and wait

ok.log: {npc} listens with the net across {his} knees. When you are done {he} is quiet a long time. "Nobody remembers," {he} says. "Except you. That is a kind of punishment. I suppose it is enough." The crack in your horn closes, slowly, over the summer.

fail.log: {npc} listens, and shrugs, and goes back to the net. "It is nothing to do with me," {he} says, which is true. Forgiveness is not owed. You lie on the bank a season anyway.

choices.text: Say nothing. Help mend the nets for a season

effects.log: You hold the net in your teeth while {npc} knots it. You never explain. At the end of the season {npc} gives you a fish and says, for no reason, "Whatever it was, it is all right." It is not enough to close the crack. It is something. (-8 health)

events.text: The king sends for you in the night. On a lacquer tray before him lies a leaf from the palace garden, and in it the insects have eaten holes, and the holes are characters: split apart, they spell nothing; put together, they spell the family name of the scholar who leads the reformers, and the words "will be king". "Heaven has written it," the king says. "I want only the beast of law to agree." The leaf smells faintly sweet.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The leaf is heaven's writing. Tell the king it was written in honey

effects.log: Someone wrote those characters on the leaf in honey, and let the insects do the rest. You say so. The king goes very still, then very red. Somebody in the hall is going to be in great trouble tonight, and for once it is the right somebody.

choices.text: Say the horn is silent

effects.log: The king does not want silence. He wants a verdict. He sends you back to the gate, and keeps the leaf in a box beside his bed, and looks at it every night.

choices.text: Agree that heaven has spoken

effects.log: The king smiles for the first time in months. In the morning there is a list.

events.text: The list comes to the gate on a lacquer tray, carried by a eunuch who will not look at you: the warrants for the scholars of the reform, and at the top of each one, stamped in red, a seal you have never seen before. It is you. A one-horned lion with its head lowered. "So the people know," the eunuch says to the paving stones, "that the beast of law agrees."

choices.text: Break the seal with your horn

ok.log: The jade seal splits on the tray in front of the whole gate. The eunuch runs. By noon the story is in every market: the haechi broke its own seal. The warrants go out anyway, unstamped, and the purge is smaller, and a great many people know exactly what it is.

fail.log: The jade is hard and your horn is not what it was. The seal is chipped, not broken, and goes out on the warrants with a notch in its horn. (-10 health)

choices.text: Lie down and let them stamp

effects.log: Forty warrants, forty red beasts with their heads lowered. Each one of them is a little bit of you.

choices.text: Walk to the reformers' houses yourself and lie down at each gate

effects.log: The soldiers who come with the warrants find a horned beast lying across the gate of the first house, and do not know what to do, and send for orders. You get to three houses before the orders come. Three families get away by the back lane.

events.text: Four scholars kneel in the yard before the gate in their white under-robes, hands bound, and the king on a dais behind you says: lower your head at the guilty. Three of them, the horn says, if it says anything, are honest men who wrote honest memorials. The fourth stole from the relief granary in a famine year, and is the one the king likes best, and has been put in the row so that you will pass over him.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The favourite swears he is clean. Lower your head at the fourth only

effects.log: You walk past three scholars and lower your head at the fourth. The king's face goes white. The three are sent home. The fourth goes to the island. You are not invited into the palace again for a hundred years.

choices.text: Lie down in front of all four, and do not move

effects.log: The king shouts. The guards prod you with spears. You lie there until sunset. The scholars are taken away anyway, to exile, not death, because the guards are too frightened of the beast to use the sword in front of it.

choices.text: Lower your head at whoever the king looks at

effects.log: The king looks at the first scholar. You lower your head. He looks at the second. Something in your horn cracks. By the fourth you cannot feel the horn at all.

events.text: Another king. Another list. You have been the seal on more than one purge now, and the histories have started to draw you on the warrants: a lion with a lowered horn, very neatly. You are tired. It would be so easy not to look, any more: only to lower your head at whoever the throne points to, for ever, and let the throne carry the weight.

choices.text: Get up and walk out of the capital, and keep walking

effects.log: You walk out of the South Gate and do not look back. For a season you eat nothing but bitter leaves in the hills and drink nothing but cold spring water, until the horn begins, faintly, to feel cold again when somebody lies.

choices.text: Go before the throne and lower your head at the king

effects.log: The whole court sees it. The king is not deposed, quite. But the list is burned, and the king lives the rest of a short reign afraid of the gate, and the next king, who was in the hall that day as a boy, never makes a list at all.

choices.text: Lower your head at whoever the throne points to

effects.log: You stop looking. The purges of the scholars go into the histories with your image on the warrant, and the scholars who survive teach their children that the haechi is a beast of the throne. They are right, by then.

events.text: A new court of new men, who believe in what can be measured. They come to the gate with a surveyor's rope and a stick marked in feet, and measure you: length, breadth, the space you take up before the gate. The processional road is to be widened for a great fair of the realm's products, and you are, the chief surveyor says to his clerk in front of you, an obstruction. "Also it is only a superstition," he adds. "The fires come from kitchens."

choices.text: (the horn: true) He believes it. Lie still and let them measure

effects.log: He is not lying. He really believes fire comes only from kitchens, and he is mostly right. You let them measure. Being disbelieved by an honest man is not the same as being wronged.

choices.text: Lie still and let them measure

effects.log: They measure you twice, because the first figure seemed too large. It was not. The clerk writes it down with a shaking hand.

choices.text: Stand up

effects.log: You stand up. You are larger standing up. The surveyor's rope is not long enough, and the clerk drops the stick, and the new men go back to their office and write that the obstruction "proved difficult to measure".

events.text: They come back with forty labourers, ropes, rollers and an order sealed by people who have never once looked at the Fire Mountain. They mean to move you aside, to the wall, out of the way of the road, and to wrap you in straw mats for the winter "to protect the stone". The labourers are frightened. One of them, an old porter, bows to you before he picks up his rope.

choices.text: Let them move you. They are only labourers

effects.log: It takes them all day. They roll you to the wall on logs and wrap you in straw mats and tie the mats with rope, and leave you leaning against the bricks with your face to the wall. You cannot see the Fire Mountain from here.

choices.text: Refuse to be moved. Be heavier than forty men

ok.log: Forty men, ropes, rollers, all day. You do not move a hair. At sunset the labourers sit down on the paving and laugh, helplessly, and the old porter offers you a piece of his rice cake. The order is quietly withdrawn.

fail.log: You hold for a morning. By the afternoon they have brought oxen. You are rolled to the wall and wrapped in straw and tied, and you can no longer see the mountain.

choices.text: Ring the bell once, for the labourers only

effects.log: A soft note only the forty of them hear. They understand. They move you slowly, and carefully, and when they wrap you in straw they leave a gap in the mats at your face, facing south, and the old porter checks it every week.

events.text: Winter, and you are wrapped in straw by a wall, and the city burns. Not once: a string of fires, a granary in the east market, a row of houses by the canal, the new court's own records office, one after another all winter. The people stand in the smoke and look at the empty place before the gate, and then at the bundle of straw by the wall, and say out loud that it is because the haechi was moved.

choices.text: Shrug off the mats in the night and walk back to your place

effects.log: At midnight the straw falls off you in a heap and you walk back across the square and lie down before the gate where you belong, face to the south. In the morning the new men find you there. Nobody, after that winter, is willing to sign the order to move you again.

choices.text: Walk out and swallow the fires one by one, wrapped as you are

effects.log: A beast in a coat of burning straw goes from fire to fire all night, swallowing them. By dawn the mats are ash and so are you, nearly. The people carry you back to the gate on a door, forty of them, and the old porter is at the front. (-25 health)

choices.text: Stay in the straw. Let the new men learn

effects.log: You stay wrapped, face to the wall. The fires go on all winter, and the people go on saying it is because the haechi was moved, and the new men go on saying it is kitchens, and both of them are partly right. The mats rot and are replaced, and rot and are replaced. Nobody moves you back while you are still a beast who could see.

events.text: Twenty years after the winter of fires, the new court has grown old and become simply the court, and a minister who was a boy that winter has a petition drawn up: that the haechi be restored, by ceremony, to its place before the gate, and the space before it kept clear for ever. He comes to read it to you first. He reads well.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to him

effects.log: He finishes reading and finds the beast he has been reading to bowing to him. He goes home and tells nobody, and keeps the petition's first draft in a box, and his grandchildren find it.

choices.text: Ask him whether he believes it, or only remembers it

effects.log: "I remember the fires," he says. "And I remember you were moved. I do not know which came first. I am not sure it matters." The horn agrees with him, which surprises you both.

events.text: {npc}, an alchemist of a dark sect, comes to the gate in the robe of a pilgrim and sits down beside you as if to rest. "I will be honest with you," {he} says, "because you would know if I were not. My sect will pay any price for a sliver of your horn. Ground fine, they say, it lets the drinker see lies. A sliver. You would never miss it."

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The powder lets the drinker see lies. Tell {him} what it really does

effects.log: You tell {npc} what the horn tells you: that a haechi's horn ground in a mortar does not make anyone see lies. It makes them see liars, everywhere, in everyone. {npc} goes pale. {He} had a sliver from a dead haechi's horn once, and drank it, and has not trusted {his} own reflection since.

choices.text: Say no

effects.log: {npc} nods as if {he} had expected it, and goes. The next week there are men with nets in the inn by the South Gate asking which hour the haechi sleeps.

choices.text: Lower your head at {him}

effects.log: {npc} goes backwards into the gutter with a cry. {He} was not lying about the price. {He} was lying about the sect, which has already sent its hunters.

events.text: A door you have not felt before opens in the paint: a courtroom far in the hills, a wall freshly painted with a judge and a horned beast, and in the painted room a woman calling for help. You step through. The courtroom is a ruined hall. The painting is three days old. The woman is gone, and the floor is a net, and the walls are full of men with hooked poles.

choices.text: Break the net and fight your way out

ok.log: Silk net, iron hooks, thirty sect hunters. You go through the net horn first and through the wall after it, and the hall comes down behind you. The sect does not paint another false courtroom for years.

fail.log: The hooks get into your scales. You tear free in the end, leaving blood and a handful of mane in the net, and go back into the paint bleeding. They have a lock of your mane now. They will be back.
fail.deathCause: a sect's net in a false courtroom

choices.text: Step back into the fresh paint before it closes

ok.log: The paint is still wet. You go back into it like a swimmer going under, and the hunters' hooks close on a wall with a picture on it, and the picture is laughing.

fail.log: The paint has dried at the edges. You get through, scraped raw along both flanks. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lie down in the net and wait for whoever comes to the mortar

effects.log: They truss you and carry you down the hill on poles. Halfway down, in a village, the people see what they are carrying, and come out with hoes and sickles, and the hunters drop the poles and run. You did not know the village had a painted wall. It does. (-10 health)

events.text: News from the hills: {npc}, the master of the dark sect, drank the first of the powder made from an old haechi's horn-chip and, it is said, a lock of your mane. Since then {he} has seen a liar in every face. {He} has killed three of {his} own disciples for lying. They were not. Now {he} is coming to the capital, with the powder in a gourd at {his} belt, to look at the king.

choices.text: Meet {him} on the road and let {him} look at you

ok.log: {npc} stares at you on the road with eyes like cracked glass. "You are lying," {he} says. "Everyone is." "Then look at the water," you say, and {he} looks into a roadside puddle, and sees a liar there too, and sits down in the road and weeps, and empties the gourd into the ditch.

fail.log: {npc} sees a liar in you, too, and attacks. You knock {him} into the river. {He} goes home with the gourd still at {his} belt. (-20 health)

choices.text: Warn the palace and lie down across the gate

effects.log: {npc} reaches the gate and finds you lying across it. {He} looks at you a long time with the powder in {his} eyes, sees a liar, and does not dare. {He} turns and goes back to the hills.

events.text: The dark sect has stopped hunting you. It has done something cleverer. In a valley two days from the capital its men hold the children of a whole village in a barn, forty of them, and a message comes to the gate on an arrow: the horn, freely given, at the mortar, by the next new moon, and the children walk home. The horn tells you, when you hold the message in your teeth, that every word of it is true.

choices.text: Go to the valley and fight for the barn

ok.log: It is a long night. In the morning the barn door is open and forty children are being counted by forty frantic parents, and the dark sect's mortar is in three pieces in the stream.

fail.log: There are too many of them. You get the barn door open and the children out, and then they bring you down in the stream with hooks, and you get away only because the village comes with torches. (-35 health)
fail.deathCause: the dark sect's hooks, in a stream below a barn

choices.text: Ring the bell for the censors and the army, and go with them

effects.log: The army is slow, and you go ahead of it alone and lie down across the barn door until it comes, with hooks in your flank. Then the censors come, two hundred soldiers behind them, and the sect's men are not brave. The children walk home. The censors write the sect's crimes on a white board and hang it over the barn door, and seal the door with thorns. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go to the mortar and give them the horn

effects.log: You go. You lay your head on the edge of the stone mortar, and the children walk home in a line, and do not look back, because they have been told not to. The sect grinds the horn into a powder said to let the drinker see lies. It makes them see enemies everywhere. In three generations the sect has destroyed itself, and the powder is still being sold, a pinch at a time, in back rooms, priceless and cursed.

events.text: One evening someone is lying on the other side of the gate, where the old stone beast used to be before the carvers took it away for repairs. Grey-white, curly mane, one horn like a white candle. The haechi of the far spring. Older than when you last saw them; their horn has three rings in it you do not have. "You never came home," they say. "So I came here. The spring is looked after. My kids are grown. Shall we butt heads over nothing for a week, like we used to?"

choices.text: Yes

effects.log: A week of butting heads in the square before the gate, very gently, over nothing at all, while the officials who must dismount wait at the edge of the square with their horses and do not dare say a word.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to them

effects.log: They bow back. The officials at the dismount line, who have never seen you bow to anyone, go home and tell their households, and that winter the children of the capital play at two haechi bowing.

events.text: The haechi of the far spring has stayed. They lie on the other side of the gate, face to the south, as you do. In the dry season, with two of you watching, the Fire Mountain sulks; when it smokes, two bells ring instead of one, a fourth apart, and the whole city hears the interval and runs for buckets. People have started calling you the pair.

choices.text: Stay a pair

effects.log: The pair before the gate. The carvers come and measure both of you, and the city puts the two of you on its lanterns and its New Year pictures, always facing south, always together.

choices.text: Ask them what they see when they look at the city

effects.log: "Dry wood," they say. "And children. More children than lies, if you count properly. You have been here too long to count properly." You count again. They are right.

events.text: A cold clear evening, the Fire Mountain dark across the river, the dismount line swept, the bells at your two throats quiet. The haechi of the far spring says, without turning their head: "We could stay. Not like this, getting up and lying down. As stone. Both of us, facing south, for as long as there is a gate."

choices.text: Not yet

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. They say nothing. In the morning they are still there, which is an answer.

choices.text: Go back to the spring with them instead

effects.log: You both get up. The officials at the dismount line watch two horned beasts walk out of the North Gate together and do not know whether to be glad or afraid.

choices.text: Turn to stone together

effects.log: You lie still, side by side across the gate, and the stillness goes in and does not come out. By morning there are two stone haechi before the palace gate, faces to the south, a small bronze bell at each throat. The bells ring whenever fire comes. The capital takes the two of you for its emblem, and puts you on everything, and children who have never seen a fire know what the pair is for.

events.text: The embroiderer of the Inspector-General's badge, {npc}, is very old and nearly blind, and has sewn you onto two hundred badges in sixty years. {He} comes to the gate on a grandchild's arm with the newest one unfinished in a frame. "I cannot see the eyes any more," {he} says. "Will you lend me yours, for the eyes? Only the eyes."

choices.text: Lend {him} your sight for the eyes

effects.log: {npc} sews by feel, with your breath on {his} hands, and when {he} ties off the last thread the embroidered beast on the badge is looking at you. You are a little less clear afterwards. The badge is the best {he} ever made.

choices.text: Lie still while {he} looks at you as closely as {he} can

effects.log: {npc} puts {his} face a hand from yours and looks for an hour. Then {he} goes home and sews the eyes from memory. They are not quite right. They are very nearly right, which, the old Inspector-General says, is the most honest thing about them.

events.text: Far away, in a provincial yamen, a young inspector, {npc}, wearing the newest badge, is listening to a county magistrate explain the missing relief rice. It is a good explanation. And for the first time in {his} life {npc} feels, somewhere behind the badge on {his} chest, cold, the way water is cold: the magistrate is lying. You feel {him} feel it, from the gate.

choices.text: Make the cold a little colder

effects.log: {npc} stands up in the middle of the explanation and asks for the granary keys. The rice is in the magistrate's brother's storehouse. {npc} rides home with the badge on {his} chest and does not know why {he} keeps touching it.

choices.text: Let {npc} decide alone

effects.log: {npc} hesitates, and then asks for the keys anyway, on nothing but a feeling. You are prouder of that than of anything the badge did.

events.text: There are a thousand hats now with your face on them, and a hundred badges, and every one has a sliver of your sight in it, and every honest inspector who wears one sees, sometimes, a little. You are not as clear as you were. You could give the rest: all of it, to all of them, and lie before the gate blind, and every honest official in the land would see better for as long as there are hats.

choices.text: Keep your sight. A blind haechi sees nothing at all

effects.log: You keep it. The hats keep their slivers, and the badges theirs. It is a fair division, and the horn, which always knows, does not complain.

choices.text: Give the last of your sight away

effects.log: You close your eyes and let it go, a sliver to every hat and badge in the land. You are blind. In a thousand offices, honest inspectors look up from their papers at the same moment, puzzled, and then look back down, and see the lie in the second paragraph that they would have missed. Later lives find the badges in old chests, and some of them, put on, still go cold.

events.text: {npc}, a brewer whose family has made the clear white rice liquor of the capital for nine generations, comes to the gate at night with a spade, a lantern and three sealed jars. "My great-grandmother buried jars under you," {he} says, "to be opened in a good year. Nobody has opened them. Every year someone says this is not quite it. I am burying three more, in case. Will you keep them?"

choices.text: Lie still while {he} digs

effects.log: {npc} digs under your forepaws all night, and lowers the jars in on ropes, and fills in the earth and sweeps the paving, and by dawn the gate looks the same as always. You can feel the jars, faintly, like three cool stones in a warm bed.

choices.text: "Not yet. Almost. Wait." You have said it before

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "That is what the family says you say," {he} says, and digs anyway, and lowers the three new jars in beside the old ones. You feel them settle, cool, among the others, like new pupils taking their places at the end of a row.

choices.text: Ask {him} what a good year would be

effects.log: {npc} stops digging and leans on the spade. "My great-grandmother said: a year nobody in the land is hungry. My grandfather said: a year the king hears every drum. My mother said: a year with no great fire." {He} laughs. "I think a year all three of them would agree on."

events.text: Three ministers stand before the gate on New Year's morning, arguing in low voices over your head about whether this is the good year and the jars should come up. A victory on the northern frontier, says one. A harvest the whole land can eat, says the second. A year in which not one person has been executed, says the third, who is the youngest. Every one of them is telling the truth. Every one of them is wrong about the others.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to the youngest

effects.log: The two older ministers fall silent. The youngest goes red. The jars stay in the ground: it was not yet a year without executions. But the next year the youngest minister persuades the king to commute every sentence that reaches him, and the year after that, nearly.

choices.text: Lie still. It is not your place to say

effects.log: They argue until noon and agree that it is not quite the good year, as every generation has. You feel the jars under your paws, cool, patient, and you find you are patient too.

events.text: It is not yet the good year. You can feel it coming: not this decade, not the next, but the land is leaning toward it, like a field toward rain. You could lie down on the jars, properly, all your weight, and sleep, and wait for it, and wake only when the whole land is glad.

choices.text: Stay awake. A good year needs watching for

effects.log: You stay awake, and keep the jars cool, and watch. A good year, you suspect, is easier to have when somebody is keeping the bad ones away.

choices.text: Sleep on the jars, and wait for a good year

effects.log: You lie down on the jars and sleep. The city grows up round the gate, and changes its hats and its kings and its arguments, and every New Year three ministers stand over you and say: not quite. You do not mind. You are dreaming of the morning they say yes, and the jars come up, and the liquor inside is clear as spring water and has been waiting for exactly that.

events.text: The bronze water jars at the corners of the palace halls are low this dry year: the steward whose duty it is to fill them has been selling the water-carriers' rice and letting the jars go. The fire demon, you know, comes down off the Fire Mountain on dry nights and walks the roofs, and looks for a jar to look into. When it sees its own face, it runs. When there is no water, it sees nothing.

choices.text: Lower your head at the steward in front of the palace staff

effects.log: The steward goes down on the paving, and the water-carriers get their rice, and every jar is full by evening, brim to brim.

choices.text: Fill the jars yourself, all night

effects.log: Every jar at every corner, from the well in the back garden, a mouthful at a time. By the hour of the ox you are soaked and the jars are full, and on the ridge of the throne hall something red stops, and looks down, and sees itself, and goes back to the mountain.

events.text: You look down into a full bronze jar at the corner of the throne hall one still night and see yourself: grey-white, the horn, the ears laid back, the bell at your throat. And behind your face, very deep, as if the jar went down much further than a jar can go, there is room. Room for a beast to lie down in the water, in every jar at every corner, and look up at whatever comes to look in.

choices.text: Put your face into the water, just to see

effects.log: It is cold and clear and goes down for ever. You see the bottoms of all the jars at once, as if they were one jar. You lift your face out, dripping, and the jar is a jar again.

choices.text: Listen for the breathing you heard in the jars once

effects.log: You heard it centuries ago, lying beside the jars on a hot night: every jar breathing, very slowly, like a sleeper. It is still there. Now you know whose breath it is going to be.

choices.text: Step back. A jar is for a demon to look in

effects.log: You step back. But you know now that the room is there, and you lie at the gate thinking about it for a long time.

events.text: A dry night, a hot wind, and the fire demon on the roofs of the palace. It goes from corner to corner, to every jar, and in every jar it sees its own face and flinches, and comes back, and looks again, and gets braver each time. Ugliness, looked at often enough, stops being frightening. You could go down into the jars. Then it would look in and see you, every time, looking back.

choices.text: Stay at the gate, and ring the bell when it comes

effects.log: The bell rings on the dry nights, and the palace runs with buckets, and the jars stay full. It is the old way. It works, mostly.

choices.text: Go down into the water jars

effects.log: You go into the jar at the corner of the throne hall and do not come up, and then you are in all of them at once, at every corner of every hall. The fire demon comes to the roof, and looks in, and there is its own face, and behind its face, very deep, a beast with one horn looking back. It runs, and keeps on running, every dry night for as long as there are jars. Palace servants who fill them sometimes see, for an instant, a grey-white shape in the water, and are careful to fill them to the brim.

events.text: You dream of the spring at the edge of the world: ice on the stones, the birches, the larch, the water so clear the bottom looks close enough to touch, and a kid with a bud of horn drinking from it who might be you. You wake before the gate with the taste of snowmelt in your mouth, and the city smells of smoke and sugar and lies.

choices.text: Remember it all day

effects.log: The birches, the spring, the bitter leaf, the fox that lied to the hare. A whole day of it. By evening the city smells a little cleaner, or you do.

choices.text: Put it out of your mind. The gate is your place now

effects.log: You put it away. It does not stay away.

events.text: A message from the north, carried by a magpie that is very tired: the haechi of the far spring is old, and has kids, and the kids have no one to teach them which quarrels to walk into and which to leave alone. "Come home," the message says, in the magpie's words. "The capital has had you for ages. The spring has not."

choices.text: Send back that you are thinking about it

effects.log: The magpie flies north with your answer. It is the first time in centuries you have told someone you did not know.

choices.text: Send back no

effects.log: The magpie looks at you a long time, as magpies do, and flies north. You feel the gate under you very solid and very heavy.

events.text: You could go. Get up, walk out of the North Gate, up the rivers, across the ice, into the larch and birch, to the spring at the edge of the world, and lie down beside the haechi of the far spring, and teach the kids, and let the capital keep itself. It can. Probably. It has its painted walls, its hats, its badges, its water jars. It has had you a long time.

choices.text: Stay. The city still needs watching

effects.log: You stay. Every spring, when the wind comes from the north, you lift your head and smell the birches, very faintly, a thousand li away.

choices.text: Go home to the clear spring

effects.log: You walk out of the North Gate at dawn, and the officials at the dismount line watch you go and do not know what to do with their horses. It takes a year to reach the spring. The haechi of the far spring is waiting. Your kids are born with horns like white candles, and the frontier quarrels are settled, for a thousand years, by something nobody sees.

events.text: In heaven's archive, a clerk of the court lets you see the register of beasts, a scroll so long it is wound on a drum the size of a granary. Your own line is very long. At the very end of it, in fresh ink, a note in a hand you do not know: may be sent back to the beginning, if it asks, remembering everything.

choices.text: Ask the clerk what it means

effects.log: "It means what it says," says the clerk, who is a heron in a blue robe. "Some go back. A kid with a bud of horn at a spring at the edge of the world, knowing every lie it will ever hear. Very few ask. Most think they would be bored."

choices.text: Roll the scroll back and pretend you did not see it

effects.log: You roll it back. The ink is still fresh in your mind.

events.text: You dream of a bud of horn under curls, very small, very white, and the first time it ever rang, faintly, like ice on a spring. You dream of the fox who lied to the hare, and this time you know, before it opens its mouth, every word it will say. You wake in heaven's court with your great horn heavy on your brow, and miss the small one.

choices.text: Remember every first thing, one by one

effects.log: The first bitter leaf. The first true butt. The first lie you ever heard. They are very far away and very clear, like stones at the bottom of a spring.

choices.text: Wonder what you would do differently

effects.log: Very little, you decide. Fewer sweet grapes. One butt you would take back. One horn you would not lower, and one you would. It is a short list for so long a life.

events.text: The heron clerk finds you at the edge of the court of clouds. "The note in the register," it says. "It is still there. If you want it, say so now. You will be small, and the forest will lie to you, and you will know every lie before it is spoken, and you will have to learn all over again what to do with that."

choices.text: Say no. Once is enough, and it was a good once

effects.log: The heron bows and strikes the note out with a single neat stroke. You feel lighter, and older, and done with wishing.

choices.text: Ask to be sent back

effects.log: A clear spring at the edge of the world. Ice on the stones, birches in snow, and on the moss beside the water a kid with scales like frost and a bud of horn under its curls. Somewhere nearby a fox is telling a hare the river is frozen. You know it is lying. You know everything. You lie in the moss and laugh, in a small voice, and begin again.

events.text: The summons comes on a morning of no wind: a heron in a blue robe, standing on the dismount line, holding a tablet of white jade. You are called up. Not to be judged: to sit. You climb a stair of cloud that starts behind the palace gate where nobody in the capital can see it, and at the top is a court as wide as a province, and at the far end of it a judgement seat, and at the foot of the seat, a place exactly the shape of a beast with one horn, lying down.

choices.text: Lie down in your place

effects.log: It fits, as the word for law fitted. The judge of heaven, whose face is too bright to see, puts down one hand and rests it, very briefly, between your ears. Then the first case is called.

choices.text: Stop at the foot of the stair and look back at the capital first

effects.log: The city is very small from here, and very dry, and very dear. Then you climb the rest of the way and lie down in your place, and the court, which waited for you without a word, begins.

events.text: The first great case: a kingdom below has had seven years of drought, and its king has beaten the drum of heaven until the royal hands bled. The envoy of the Jade court who carried the decree of drought, {npc}, stands under oath before the seat in robes like a sunset and explains, smiling, that the drought was punishment for the kingdom's impiety, duly decided and duly sent. The court murmurs approval. The envoy has a lovely voice.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The drought was duly decided. Lower your head at the envoy

effects.log: The horn goes cold the moment {npc} says "duly". The drought was never decided. {npc} was paid in rain by a rival kingdom's dragon king to send it, and wrote the decree afterwards. The court goes silent. The judge of heaven looks at the envoy for the first time, and the envoy stops smiling.

choices.text: Ask to see the decree

ok.log: The decree is brought. The ink is fresher than the drought. {npc} smiles harder, and then not at all.
