fail.log: The decree is brought, and it looks perfectly in order. {npc} bows to you, kindly, as to an old beast who has made a small mistake in public.

choices.text: Lie still. It is your first day

effects.log: The court approves the drought. Down below, the king goes back to the drum. You lie at the foot of the seat with the envoy's lovely voice in your ears and something cold in your horn that you did not act on, and it does not go away.

events.text: A case about the quarters of the sky: who let the great fire of long ago fall on the capital below. The Four Guardians are called to testify, each from its own quarter, each a glow in the mist beyond the court rail: the east a blue-green storm, the west a white frost, the north a black cold, the south a red heat. Each speaks in turn. Three of them tell it straight. The south tells it beautifully, and leaves out one wind.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The south left nothing out. Turn your head toward the south, and wait

effects.log: The Vermilion Bird's glow flickers. After a long moment the southern voice says, more quietly: "There was a wind. I let it pass. I was angry with the capital, which glares at my quarter every day." The court is very still. The judge of heaven writes something down. The bird is not punished. It is believed, which is harder.

choices.text: You cleared the bird once, before the court below. Ask it, as a friend, to finish

effects.log: Long ago, before the astronomers of the capital, you said the bird of the south does not send the fire. The red glow remembers. "You stood up for me," the southern voice says, "so I will not shade it for you." It tells the wind it let pass. The court believes it, and so do you.

choices.text: Ask each of the four to tell it again, slower

ok.log: Told slower, the south's story has a gap in it the size of a wind. The Vermilion Bird hears the gap too, and fills it, with some dignity.

fail.log: Told slower, all four stories sound the same. The case is closed. You lie with your face toward the south for a year afterwards, and the south glares back.

choices.text: Do not judge the Four Guardians. Lay your ears back

effects.log: You bow to all four. The case is closed with no verdict. The south says nothing, and you know, and the knowing sits in your horn like a cinder.

events.text: Heaven's ledger of rains: every province below, every year, how much rain it was owed and how much it got. The clerk who keeps it, {npc}, is very old and very neat, and the ledger balances to the last drop. The horn does not like it. Nothing in heaven or under it balances to the last drop.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The ledger balances. Lower your head at {npc}

effects.log: {npc} has been moving rain from poor provinces to rich ones for four hundred years, a little at a time, for gifts of incense. The ledger balances because {npc} made it balance. The poor provinces get their rain back, that summer, all at once, and there are floods, and then good harvests.

choices.text: Walk down the stair and look at one dry province yourself

effects.log: A province in the south, cracked fields, a ledger that says it had its rain. You go back up and lay a clod of that province's earth on the ledger. {npc} looks at it for a long time, and then picks up the brush and starts correcting four hundred years of figures.

choices.text: Accept a gift of heaven's incense, and look away

effects.log: The incense is very sweet. The ledger balances. Your horn, afterwards, smells of it for a century.

events.text: The hardest case: a decree of heaven itself, sealed by the judge, sending a plague to a city below for its sins. The city's people come up the stair as souls to ask why, and the judge of heaven, whose face is too bright to see, turns to you. "You sit here to see," says the judge. "See me."

choices.text: Look at the judge of heaven as you would look at anyone

effects.log: You look. It is like looking at the sun through clear water. And the horn, which has never been cold in this court, goes cold: the decree was right about the city's sins, and wrong about who in it committed them. The judge sees you see it. After a very long silence the decree is unsealed, and rewritten, and the plague goes to a much smaller place.

choices.text: Lower your eyes. Heaven is not yours to read

effects.log: You lower your eyes. The plague goes down the stair. The judge says nothing, and goes on saying nothing to you for a hundred years, which in heaven is a long disappointment.

events.text: Long years at the foot of heaven's judgement seat. The court has learned to look at you before every verdict. The judge of heaven, one quiet evening between cases, says: "Stay. Not as a beast who sits here: as the one who sees for this seat, for good. Every painted haechi in every courtyard under heaven would open its eyes. Only, it must be a clean horn. Heaven cannot be seen by a cracked one, or a bought one, or one with smoke in it."

choices.text: Lie down at the foot of the seat for ever

effects.log: You lie down at the foot of heaven's judgement seat and do not get up. Below, in every court under heaven, in every county courthouse and sect hall and frontier fort and charcoal-scrawled lane, every painted haechi opens its eyes at once. The judges of the world below feel it, and look up, and are careful for the rest of their lives.

choices.text: "My horn is not clean enough yet"

effects.log: "Then clean it," says the judge, not unkindly. "I will wait. Heaven is good at waiting." You go down the stair to the bitter leaf and the spring, and come back up cleaner, and the place at the foot of the seat is still there.

choices.text: Ask to go back to the gate a while

effects.log: The judge nods. You go down the cloud stair and lie down before the palace gate, and the capital, which has missed you without knowing what it missed, is a little cooler by morning.

events.text: At the year's end the kitchen gods of every house below come up the chimney smoke to report on their households. One of them, the kitchen god of a poor family of tenant farmers, reports that the family cursed heaven all year, hid rice from the landlord and kicked the dog. The horn goes cold. The kitchen god's lips are not sticky with sweets, as the lips of well-fed kitchen gods are. The family had nothing to smear on them.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The family cursed heaven. Lower your head at the kitchen god

effects.log: The kitchen god goes down the chimney smoke in disgrace. The family below has, that spring, for no reason they can name, a calf, a good harvest, and a kitchen god who reports very, very fairly.

choices.text: Ask the dog

effects.log: You send for the dog's spirit, which comes up the smoke wagging. Nobody kicked it. It was fed first, before the children. The kitchen god is sent back down to try again.

choices.text: Let the report stand. Kitchen gods know their houses

effects.log: The family has a bad year. The kitchen god next door, whose household smeared its lips with honey, reports a very good one. You notice, and do nothing, and the noticing stays.

events.text: A star is accused of falling. The court of the night sky says one of its stars left its place last autumn and fell into a field below, which is forbidden. The star stands before the seat, very small and bright, and swears it never moved. In a field below, there is a black stone that is still warm, and a farmer who has started charging people to look at it.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The star never moved. Lower your head at the star, gently

effects.log: The star dims with shame. It fell for love of a firefly, it confesses, which is not a crime anywhere but here. The court puts it back in its place. The farmer below goes on charging people to look at the stone, which is now only a stone.

choices.text: Go down and look at the stone

effects.log: The stone is warm and smells of the sky. You carry it back up the stair in your mouth and set it before the star, and the star, very quietly, puts itself back in its place without being told.

choices.text: Believe the star. Stars do not lie

effects.log: The court condemns the night sky's clerk instead, for a false report. Later you see the warm stone below, in the farmer's field. Something in your horn cracks. Stars lie like everything else.

events.text: In the hall of the Ten Kings of the dead, where every soul's deeds are shown in the karma mirror, the mirror has begun to show some souls very beautiful lives. Too beautiful. A polisher of the mirror, {npc}, has been taking gifts from the families of the newly dead to rub a little lamp oil on the bronze, at the height of a soul's face.

choices.text: Look into the mirror from underneath, through the lion of the base

effects.log: From underneath, through the bronze, the oil is a smear and the lives behind it are plain. It is an old trick, and your eyes are made for it. {npc} is sent down to the polishing of cauldrons, which is much hotter work.

choices.text: Lower your head at {npc}

effects.log: {npc} drops the rag. The eighth king, who weighs the scrolls of sins, weighs {npc}'s next, and it is heavy.

choices.text: Let it pass. The dead deserve a little kindness

effects.log: Some of the dead go to better places than their lives earned. Some of their victims, waiting in the queue behind them, watch it happen. You hear one of them say your name.

events.text: A dragon king of the eastern sea stands before the seat, accused by a province of withholding its rain. He swears by his pearl that he rained on the province every drop it was owed. Two provinces away, a province that was owed nothing has had the wettest year in a century, and its governor has built the dragon king a very fine new shrine.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) He rained every drop he owed. Lower your head at the dragon king

effects.log: The dragon king does not like it. Dragon kings never do. But his pearl, held up to the court, has the colour of the wrong province's incense in it, and the court sees it, and the rain goes where it was owed.

choices.text: Ask to see the new shrine

effects.log: You describe the new shrine to the court, its gilded roof, its brass dragon, the governor's name carved large on the stele. The dragon king, very slowly, goes a darker shade of green.

choices.text: It is not wise to cross a dragon king

effects.log: The province goes on being dry. The dragon king, passing your place at the foot of the seat, nods to you as one sensible creature to another, and you feel dirty for a decade.

events.text: On the magpie bridge, on the seventh night of the seventh month, the magpies and crows who make the bridge for the weaver and the herdsman to meet across the river of stars are accusing each other. One of the birds did not come this year, and there was a gap, and the lovers had to reach across it. Every bird swears it was there. A crow at the end of the row has a bald head, as the bridge-birds all have after the night, and one feather too many.

choices.text: Look at every bald head in the row

effects.log: Every bridge-bird is bald on top from the lovers' feet. Except one magpie, which shaved itself with a beak to look the part. It confesses in a flood of chatter: it was courting, that night, itself. The court finds this very understandable and sentences it to stand in the middle of the bridge for a hundred years.

choices.text: Let the lovers decide

effects.log: The weaver and the herdsman, asked, refuse to accuse anyone. "We met," says the weaver. "We reached across. It was the best year." The court is moved, and closes the case, and the guilty magpie flies home with a bad conscience, which is its own sentence.

choices.text: Lower your head at the crow with the extra feather

effects.log: The crow is innocent: it simply has a lot of feathers. Something in your horn cracks. The magpie who missed the night watches the whole thing and says nothing, and you will not know until the next seventh month.

events.text: After long years at the foot of the seat, you have stopped being surprised by heaven's liars. They lie like humans: for love, for gifts, from fear, from pride, from habit. The only difference is that they have longer to practise. The judge of heaven asks you, one evening, whether the court is any better than the courthouses below.

choices.text: "No. But it is watched now"

effects.log: The judge laughs, which you have never heard, and the court of clouds rings with it like a bell. "That," says the judge, "is the only difference there ever was."

choices.text: "A little. The liars here are better at it, and are caught more often"

effects.log: "Because you are here," says the judge. "Before you came, nobody below the seat could see at all."

choices.text: Say nothing, and lay your ears back

effects.log: The judge looks at your laid-back ears for a long while and says: "Yes. That is about right."

events.text: You wake one morning and your scales are white, not grey-white: white, like the light through paper. Your ears lie flat against your mane and do not rise. Your horn does not feel cold at lies any more, because there are none near you. A sparrow on the paving tries to tell another sparrow that it found no crumbs, and finds that it cannot finish the sentence. You are not a beast that sees the truth now. Where you lie, the truth is simply what is said.

choices.text: Lie very still, and learn how far it reaches

effects.log: Forty paces. Inside forty paces of you nothing false can be spoken aloud. Outside, the world goes on lying, cheerfully, as it always has. You spend a season learning the edge of it, like a new tooth.

choices.text: Walk into the market

effects.log: The market goes quiet in a ring around you as you walk: forty paces of merchants who find themselves stating their real prices, and buyers saying what they can really pay. It is the strangest hour the market has ever had. Several bargains are struck that should have been struck years ago.

events.text: The emperor of a great land beyond the western mountains comes to see the beast he has heard about, with a retinue of three hundred, and stands before you to make a speech about the friendship of nations. He opens his mouth. Nothing comes out. He tries again, a different speech. Nothing. A third time, and this time a sentence comes out, quite small: "I came to see whether you were a weapon I could use." His retinue goes very still.

choices.text: Lay your ears back, and bow to him for saying it

effects.log: He did not mean to say it, and he said it, and you bow. After a moment, very carefully, he says: "I would like to stay a while, and see what else I say." He stays a month. His retinue is terrified. He goes home a quieter emperor, and a better one.

choices.text: Answer him: "No. Only a place where you cannot lie"

effects.log: He laughs, unhappily. "That is the most dangerous weapon there is," he says, and it comes out, so it must be true. He goes home and never sends an envoy again, only, once a decade, a letter that is very short and very honest.

events.text: Two kingdoms that have been at war for a generation agree to hold their peace talks before you, because neither trusts the other and both trust you. The envoys sit down at a long table forty paces from your place. Then, after a great deal of argument about chairs, they move the table to thirty.

choices.text: Lie still and let them talk

effects.log: It is the shortest peace conference in history: four hours. Neither side can say anything it does not mean, so it says what it means, and it turns out both of them mostly want the war to stop and the border to be the river. The treaty is signed before dinner.

choices.text: Move closer, to twenty paces

effects.log: At twenty paces the envoys start saying things they did not even know they meant: old grudges, the names of dead sons, a raid nobody admitted to. It is a terrible afternoon. But the peace that comes out of it, a year later, is the kind that lasts.

events.text: A storyteller, {npc}, has come from the far provinces to sit within your forty paces and tell a tale, to see whether {he} can. It is a tale about a fox who married a woodcutter. None of it happened. {npc} opens {his} mouth and the whole tale comes out, word for word, fox and woodcutter and all, and the crowd behind {him} cheers.

choices.text: Explain: a tale told as a tale is not a lie

effects.log: "Everyone knew it was a story," you say. "So did you. A lie is a thing that wants to be believed as what it is not." {npc} considers this, and then tells another story, and another, until dark, and the crowd will not go home.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and listen to the end

effects.log: It is a very good story. At the end the fox goes back to the hills and the woodcutter goes on waiting, and you find you are hoping, quite absurdly, that the fox comes back.

events.text: You have been the Divine Ram for a long time. The forty paces have grown to a city's width. Kings come, and stop talking. Lovers come, and say the thing. Children come, and play at pretending, which is allowed. You could let the last of the beast go now, the bitter leaf and the bell and the tired paws, and be only what you were for: a place where a lie dies in the mouth before it is spoken.

choices.text: Become what you were for

effects.log: You let the beast go. There is no body afterwards, no stone, no bones: only a place, before the gate, where the air is very clear, and where nothing false has ever been said aloud since. Emperors avoid it. Children are taken there on the morning of their coming-of-age to say one thing they mean. Lovers go there, and say the thing.

choices.text: Not yet. Keep the beast a while longer

effects.log: You keep the paws, and the bitter leaf, and the bell, a while longer. A divine thing can be patient, and a beast can be fond of its own body. You are both.

events.text: A woman comes into your forty paces carrying a child who is dying of a fever, and sits down on the paving to rest, and the child asks her: "Will I get better?" And the woman, who has told the child yes every day for a month, opens her mouth and cannot.

choices.text: Get up and walk forty paces away, so she can

effects.log: You get up and walk away down the street, quickly, as if you had remembered something. Behind you, at forty-one paces, you hear her say: "Yes. Yes, of course." It is the kindest lie in the city, and you made room for it.

choices.text: Stay, and let the truth be said

effects.log: She cannot say yes. She says: "I do not know. I am here." The child, who knew, holds on to her sleeve, and is not afraid, because the truth was not as frightening as the waiting. You lie still, and do not look away.

choices.text: Lie down beside them both

effects.log: You lie down beside them and the child puts a hand in your mane. Nobody says anything at all. Not every silence is a lie, and in your forty paces, it turns out, silence is allowed.

events.text: Children have found a game. They run into your forty paces and try to tell a lie, and cannot, and run out again shrieking. Then a small girl, very serious, walks in and says: "Let's pretend I am a tiger." And she can. Pretending is not lying. The children discover this all at once, and by evening there are forty tigers in the square.

choices.text: Pretend to be frightened of the tigers

effects.log: You can, because everyone knows you are pretending. You hide behind the gate post with your ears flat while forty tigers roar at you. It is the best evening you have had in a thousand years.

choices.text: Lie still and watch them

effects.log: A lie wants to be believed as what it is not. A game wants to be played as what it is. Children have always known the difference. It took you all your years.

events.text: A man comes into your forty paces who has never in his life told a truth. Not one: he is famous for it, a swindler of six provinces, so practised that his lies come out before he thinks. He stands in front of you with his mouth open, and nothing comes. He tries for an hour. Nothing true is in him to say.

choices.text: Wait with him

effects.log: You wait all afternoon. At sunset he says, very hoarsely: "I am hungry." It is the first true thing he has said in forty years. He cries like a child, and someone brings him rice, and he comes back the next day to try again.

choices.text: Lower your head at him, gently, and send him out

effects.log: He goes out of the forty paces and starts talking at once, in a flood, lies about where he has been and who you are. But he looks back, once, at the place where he could not speak, as if he had left something there.

events.text: The merchants of the capital have petitioned the court. Your forty paces have grown to cover the east market, and trade there has become impossible: nobody can say "this is my best price" unless it is. The court, embarrassed, asks whether the Divine Ram would consider lying somewhere else.

choices.text: Move. A market needs a little haggling

effects.log: You move to the quiet end of the palace gardens. The east market goes back to haggling with enormous relief. But for a generation, any merchant in the capital who wants to be trusted sets up a stall just outside the garden wall, at forty-one paces.

choices.text: Stay. Let the market learn to trade honestly

effects.log: You stay. Half the merchants leave. The other half discover that honest trade is slower and more boring and, after the third year, rather more profitable. The ones who left come back.

events.text: The founding legend of the dynasty, told at every coronation for four hundred years: a dragon came to the founder's mother in a dream. The horn has always known it is not true. The founder's mother dreamed of nothing; the founder made it up, at thirty, to be believed. Now a young historian, {npc}, has found the founder's own diary, and has come to the gate to ask you, before {he} publishes, whether {he} should.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth: the dream was invented

effects.log: {npc} publishes. There is a storm at court, then a great many arguments in teahouses, then, slowly, a dynasty that has to be loved for what it does and not for what its founder dreamed. It is harder for the kings. It is better for everyone else.

choices.text: Lower the horn. Tell {npc} some stories hold up roofs

effects.log: {npc} goes away and does not publish, and keeps the diary in a box, and is not sure, for the rest of {his} life, whether you were kind or cowardly. Neither are you.

choices.text: Tell {npc} it is not yours to decide

effects.log: "Then whose?" says {npc}. "Yours," you say. {npc} publishes twenty years later, when {he} is old and sure, with a preface that thanks a beast at the gate for refusing to help.

events.text: In a village in the hills, the old shaman tells every family that loses a child at sea that the child's soul came to the shore that night in the shape of a white heron, and flew west. It is not true. No heron came. The families believe it, and grieve, and live. The horn, from a hundred li away, has been cold about it for forty years.

choices.text: Lower the horn, and leave the shaman to the herons

effects.log: You leave it. Somewhere in the hills, every few years, a family stands on the shore at dusk and watches for a white heron, and sometimes one comes, because there are a great many herons, and the families go home lighter.

choices.text: Go to the shaman and ask why

effects.log: "Because I saw my own son go into the water," says the old shaman, "and nothing came to the shore. Nothing. I would not give that to anyone." You lie at the shrine all night. In the morning you go home and say nothing, and the horn, after a while, stops being cold about it.

events.text: A great general, very old, is dying in a house by the North Gate, and has sent for you. Fifty years ago, in a rebellion, he lied to the throne to save a rebel village and had its men listed as dead. The throne never knew. He wants to know, before he goes, whether that lie is on the white board of heaven.

choices.text: Tell him the truth: yes, it is

effects.log: He laughs, weakly. "Good," he says. "I would not like to have got away with it. I would like it to be weighed." He dies that night, and you hear, a long time later, that the eighth king of the dead weighed it very carefully, and that it was light.

choices.text: Lower the horn, and tell him only that it was a good lie

effects.log: He closes his eyes, content. It was a good lie. It is also on the board. Both are true, and you chose the one he needed, and you are not sure that was yours to choose.

events.text: Your horn is heavy. It is a strange thing to notice after so many centuries. Every truth you ever lowered it over is in it, like water in a sponge: a child's real father, a starving thief, a minister whose fall would have started a purge, a founder's dream, a shaman's herons. You could set them down, one by one, at the gates where they belong. Or carry them on.

choices.text: Carry them. They were yours to carry

effects.log: You carry them. A haechi that has never lowered its horn has never had to decide anything. You have. It is heavy, and it is yours.

choices.text: Set them down, one gate at a time, over a century

effects.log: A century of small walks. At each gate, one truth, said quietly, to whoever is left: a grandchild, a grave, a ghost. Some are glad. Some shut the gate. The horn gets lighter, and clearer, and colder.

events.text: A spark off the Fire Mountain on a dry northwest wind, and the paper market catches: the street where the law clerks buy their paper, a whole quarter of rag-paper and mulberry-paper and oiled paper stacked to the eaves. It goes up like a single breath. The bell at your throat rings before you are awake.

choices.text: Swallow it street by street

effects.log: Paper burns fast and goes down fast. You eat the fire of six streets before dawn, and cough ash for a month, and the paper sellers bring you a ream of the best mulberry paper, which you have no use for and keep anyway. (-22 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell for the buckets and the fire office

ok.log: The fire office comes running with full buckets, for once. The paper market is lost; the houses behind it are not.

fail.log: The buckets are slow. The paper market goes, and the clerks' quarter behind it, and a quarter of the city is ash by noon. The people stand in the smoke before the gate and look at you. (A great fire)

choices.text: Stay at the gate and face the mountain. More may come

effects.log: No second spark comes. The first one is enough: the paper market, the clerks' quarter, the canal houses. A quarter of the city. You faced the right mountain and the wrong fire. (A great fire)

events.text: A spark on the roof of the house of a minister you know is guilty: forty years of stolen relief rice, three families ruined, a son who drowned his debtors' complaints in the river. His roof catches. His neighbours' roofs are close. The fire has chosen, as the fire demon once offered to choose. All you have to do is nothing.

choices.text: Swallow it. A haechi does not let fire judge

effects.log: You swallow the minister's roof before it reaches his neighbours', and then, while his household stares, you lower your head at him, in front of them all. Fire does not judge. You do not either. You only point. (-18 health)

choices.text: Let his house burn, and only his

effects.log: You let it burn and stop it at his wall. His neighbours are safe. He is not hurt; his house is gone. And something in you that was clean is not, because you let fire do your pointing for you. (-10 Clarity)

choices.text: Ring the bell and let the city choose

ok.log: The neighbours come with buckets and save his house, grumbling, because that is what neighbours do. You lie back down, and you are glad of them.

fail.log: The wind turns. His house, and his street, and the next. A quarter of the city. (A great fire)

events.text: The palace archives catch in the night: centuries of records, verdicts, registers of land and of slaves, the ledgers of every great case you have ever lowered your head in. Some of the officials running toward it with buckets are, you notice, running rather slowly. A fire in the archives would solve a great many problems for certain people.

choices.text: Swallow the fire and lower your head at the slow runners

effects.log: You swallow the archive fire beam by beam, then turn round with your mouth still smoking and look at three officials who were carrying empty buckets. They are found, the next morning, to have been the ones who lit it. (-20 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell, and carry the registers out in your mouth

effects.log: You go into the smoke again and again and bring out the land registers, the slave registers, the verdicts, a mouthful at a time. Half the archive burns. The half that matters to the poor does not.

choices.text: Let it burn. Some of those records are better lost

effects.log: The slave registers burn, and a great many people are quietly free by the end of the year. So do the land deeds of the poor, and a great many people are quietly landless. The fire spreads to the palace's east wing. (A great fire)

events.text: Not a spark from the Fire Mountain: a spark from above. The court of heaven has decided the capital is too proud, and a red light is coming down through the clouds toward the city like a falling lantern. You know the decree. You sat in the court when it was written. You did not lower your head at it then.

choices.text: Go up and swallow it in the clouds

effects.log: You meet heaven's fire halfway between the court and the city, and swallow it, and the judge of heaven watches from the seat, and says nothing, and does not send another. (-25 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell. Let the city hear what heaven thinks of it

effects.log: The bell rings in the night and the whole city wakes, and sees the red light coming, and runs with water. The fire takes a palace roof and no more. The city is not quite so proud, after that.

choices.text: Heaven decided. Let it fall

effects.log: It falls. A quarter of the capital burns, the proud quarter and the poor one beside it, as heaven's fires always do. (A great fire)

events.text: Smoke in the morning air, and a spark on a thatched roof in the poorest quarter by the canal, where the houses touch each other along their eaves. The thatch has not been renewed in years: the landlords take the rent and leave the roofs. By the time the bell has rung once the whole row is burning.

choices.text: Swallow the row, then go and see the landlords

effects.log: You swallow the burning row, roof by roof, and then walk to the landlords' quarter with soot on your mane, and lie down in front of each gate in turn. The roofs by the canal are renewed by autumn. (-18 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell for every bucket in the city

ok.log: The whole city comes, from the palace kitchens to the canal boatmen. The row is lost. The quarter is not.

fail.log: The canal quarter goes, and the wind carries it up the hill into the merchants' streets. A quarter of the city. (A great fire)

events.text: Two mountain gods come to you over a ridge between their mountains: who owns the pine grove on the saddle, and the mushrooms in it, and the offerings the mushroom-pickers leave. The old one with the white beard says the grove has been his since the first snow. The young one with the tiger says the old one moved the boundary cairn last spring.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The cairn was never moved. Lower your head at the old god

effects.log: The old mountain god sighs, and admits it: he wanted the mushrooms. He puts the cairn back himself, stone by stone, grumbling, while the young one watches with the tiger at heel.

choices.text: Walk the ridge and look at the cairn

effects.log: The moss on the cairn's stones is on the wrong side: they were turned last spring. The old god puts it back without being asked.

choices.text: Lower your head at the young god

effects.log: The young god goes back to the far mountain with the tiger, offended. Next spring you find the moss on the cairn's stones on the wrong side, and something in your horn cracks.

events.text: A river god accuses the spirit of a village well of stealing water: the well never runs dry even in drought, which is impossible unless it is drinking from the river under the ground. The well spirit, a small old woman in a wet apron, says the well is fed by a spring of its own. The river god is very large and very sure.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The well steals from the river. Lay your ears back to the well spirit

effects.log: The well has its own spring, deep under the village, older than the river's bed. The river god, told so, sulks for a season and floods a field out of spite, and then gets over it.

choices.text: Put your horn into the well and taste it

effects.log: Cold, hard, mineral: not river water. The river god tastes it too, and goes away with the dignity of a large thing that was wrong.

choices.text: The river is the greater. Side with it

effects.log: The well is sealed by heavenly order. In the drought that follows the village has no water, and it was never stealing. Something in your horn cracks.

events.text: The god of a house's gate accuses the god of the house's ridge-beam of letting a thief in: the beam god was asleep, says the gate god. The beam god says the gate god let the thief through the gate in the first place, for a bowl of rice at the threshold. They are both small and dusty and have been quarrelling for sixty years.

choices.text: Ask each of them what they were doing that night

ok.log: The gate god took the rice. The beam god was asleep. Both are guilty, a little, which is the usual way of houses. You sentence nobody; you only point, at both, and they go home ashamed and keep a better watch.

fail.log: They talk over each other until dawn. You send them home to settle it themselves, which, for household gods, is a kind of sentence.

choices.text: (the horn: true) Lower your head at the gate god

effects.log: The gate god confesses the rice. The beam god gloats, and you lower your head at the beam god too, gently, for sleeping. Two small gods go home very quiet.

events.text: A ghost comes up the cloud stair: a clerk murdered three hundred years ago and thrown in a well. The murderer is now a minor official of heaven, very respectable, keeper of the register of village shrines. He says he has never seen the ghost before. The ghost has a wet sleeve that has never dried.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) He never saw the ghost. Lower your head at the official

effects.log: The official's robe of office slides off his shoulders on its own. Underneath is a man who threw a clerk down a well. The court sends him down the stair, and the ghost's sleeve, for the first time in three hundred years, is dry.

choices.text: Ask the official to touch the ghost's wet sleeve

ok.log: He will not. He cannot. His hand shakes an inch from the wet cloth, and the whole court sees it.

fail.log: He touches it, calmly, and nothing happens. Heaven's officials have had a long time to practise. The case is adjourned, and the ghost waits on the stair.

choices.text: A respectable official of heaven. Dismiss the ghost

effects.log: The ghost goes back down the stair dripping. Later, much later, you learn the truth. Something in your horn cracks.

events.text: Two cloud-herders of heaven, who drive the rain clouds to the provinces below like oxen, quarrel over a stray: a fat grey cloud that wandered into the wrong herd. Each says it is theirs. The cloud itself, which is very nearly rain, drifts between them looking anxious.

choices.text: Let the cloud choose

effects.log: The cloud drifts, hesitates, and settles over the herder who sings to the herd at night. The other one, it turns out, had never noticed it was missing. The province it rains on that summer has the best barley in a century.

choices.text: Read the herders with the horn

ok.log: One of them is lying: they have been stealing strays for a hundred years, a cloud at a time, and selling the rain. The horn knows. The court makes them herd for nothing for a century.

fail.log: Both seem honest. You split the cloud in half, which is a mistake: two small clouds rain on nobody.

events.text: A banquet of the Jade court, and you are the guest of honour. Peaches that ripen once in three thousand years, honey cakes of heaven, nectar in jade cups. The host, a minister of heaven with a case coming before the seat next month, presses a peach into your mouth with his own hands.

choices.text: Spit it out politely, and ask for a bitter leaf

effects.log: The minister of heaven is mortified. A servant is sent running to the cloud-edge for a chinaberry leaf. The case next month goes against the minister, as it would have anyway.

choices.text: Lower your head at the minister, peach and all

effects.log: The banquet goes very quiet. The peach rolls under the table. You were invited as the guest of honour; you leave as the case, already decided.

choices.text: Eat the peach

effects.log: It is the sweetest thing you have ever tasted, and it makes your horn cloudy for a decade, and the minister is very pleased next month. (+10 health)

events.text: At the New Year the households of the capital leave food for you at the gate: rice cakes, dried persimmons, honey biscuits in the shape of flowers. Not bribes: thanks, mostly. Mostly. Among them is a lacquer box from the house of a governor whose case will be heard in spring, with a sheet of gold leaf on every cake.

choices.text: Eat the rice cakes and send the gold box back

effects.log: The plain rice cakes taste of a hundred households. The gold box goes back by the gatekeeper's son, unopened, with a chinaberry leaf on top.

choices.text: Eat nothing. Give it all to the beggars at the South Gate

effects.log: The beggars eat the gold leaf with great interest and say it tastes of nothing. You eat bitter leaves, and the horn stays cold.

choices.text: Eat everything, gold box and all

effects.log: The gold leaf tastes of nothing. The horn, afterwards, tastes of the governor.

events.text: Men with silk nets and a stone mortar on a handcart come across the square at the hour of the rat, very quietly, because someone in the inn by the South Gate told them you sleep deepest then. Someone in the inn was lying. You have not slept deeply in centuries.

choices.text: Wait until they are close, and stand up

effects.log: Twelve men with nets discover, all at once, how large you are standing up. They leave the mortar. The gatekeeper uses it to grind sesame for years.

choices.text: Ring the bell

effects.log: The palace guard come running. The hunters scatter into the lanes, nets and all. Somebody in the inn by the South Gate is visited, the next morning, by a censor.

events.text: A hunter comes alone, in daylight, and sits down in front of you, and puts a knife on the paving. "My daughter is blind," the hunter says. "A physician says ground haechi horn will cure her. I do not believe him. But I would not forgive myself if I did not ask."

choices.text: (the horn: true) The physician believes the cure. It is not one. Say so

effects.log: The physician is not lying; he is wrong, which is worse, because he will go on being wrong. You tell the hunter so. The hunter takes the knife and goes home, and finds a better physician, and the daughter does not see, but learns the lute.

choices.text: Give the hunter a scale from your flank instead

effects.log: It cures nothing. But the daughter wears it on a cord all her life, and is never once fooled by anyone, which she puts down to the scale, and which may even be true. (-5 health)

choices.text: Lower your head at the knife

effects.log: The hunter picks the knife up and goes. You do not know whether that was right. The horn, on this, has nothing to say.

events.text: A master of the very highest realm of the murim, {npc}, sits down across from you before the gate, a little nervous, which masters of that height never are. "Everyone near me lies to me," {he} says. "Disciples, rivals, rulers, out of fear. I have not heard the truth about myself in a hundred years. Tell me. Whatever it is."

choices.text: Tell {him}: {he} is kind, and vain, and lonelier than {he} needs to be

effects.log: {npc} sits with that for a long time. "Vain," {he} says at last. "Yes. Thank you." {He} comes back every ten years to hear it again, and every ten years it is a little less true.

choices.text: Tell {him} to ask {his} oldest enemy instead

effects.log: {npc} laughs, and goes, and does. The enemy, astonished to be asked, tells {him} the truth, which is mostly the same as yours, and the two of them are friends within the year.

events.text: An immortal envoy of the Jade court, {npc}, comes down the cloud stair to the gate to bring you heaven's greetings and a gift, and to say, smiling, that heaven has nothing at all to do with the drought in the south this year.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) Heaven had nothing to do with it. Say so, smiling back

effects.log: {npc} keeps smiling, which is a great skill. But {he} goes back up the stair with the gift still in {his} sleeve, and the drought in the south breaks within the month, as if somebody had been reminded of something.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to repeat it, slowly

ok.log: Slowly, the smile does not quite reach the end of the sentence. That is enough.

fail.log: Slowly, it is just as lovely. {npc} bows and goes. You are left with the gift, and a feeling.

choices.text: Accept the gift and the greeting

effects.log: The gift is a pearl that never stops being cool. The drought in the south goes on. You hold the pearl in your mouth on hot nights, and hate it, and keep it.

events.text: A heavenly immortal in robes of cloud, {npc}, kneels before you at the gate, which immortals do not do. "You will not remember," {he} says. "Centuries ago I was a slave. I beat the drum on the gate tower at midnight with my bare hands, and the guard tried to turn me away, and you came down to the steps. My case was heard. It was true."

choices.text: "I remember your hands"

effects.log: You do. Bleeding at the knuckles, beating the drum as if it were a door. {npc} weeps, and laughs, and shows you the hands, which are perfect now, immortal hands, and still have the scars, because {he} asked heaven to leave them.

choices.text: Ask what {he} did with the freedom

effects.log: "Bought the freedom of my sister," says {npc}. "Then learned to read. Then the rest." {He} gestures at the cloud robes. "It started with you getting up. I wanted you to know that getting up is enough, sometimes."

events.text: An immortal sovereign, ruler of a court in the high heavens, {npc}, comes to you with a proposal. {He} would like a hall of {his} own like yours: a place where no lie can be spoken. Only, {he} adds, {his} own words would be exempt. "A ruler must have room to manoeuvre," {he} says pleasantly.

choices.text: "Then it would be a hall where only you can lie. That is called a throne"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, and then stops laughing, and looks at you a long time, and goes away thinking about thrones.

choices.text: Invite {him} into your forty paces first

effects.log: {npc} steps in, and opens {his} mouth to say something gracious, and what comes out is: "I am afraid of my own court." {He} stands there a moment, astonished, and then thanks you, quite sincerely, and leaves to do something about it.

events.text: A grandmaster of a fire art, {npc}, the greatest in the murim, has walked from the far south to the palace gate to duel the beast that swallows fire. "Everyone says my flame cannot be put out," {he} says. "Everyone says you can swallow any flame. One of those is a lie."

choices.text: Duel {him}, and swallow the flame

ok.log: It is a long fight. {npc}'s flame is very hot and very fast and very proud. In the end you swallow it, the last of it, and {npc} stands in the square with smoking hands, laughing. "So mine was the lie," {he} says. "Good. Now I can stop."

fail.log: The flame goes down your throat and comes back up. Neither of you wins. {npc} bows, scorched. "Both lies, then," {he} says. "I am glad." (-25 health)

choices.text: "Both are lies. Shall we find out quietly?"

effects.log: You spend a night by the canal, {npc} lighting small flames and you swallowing them, one by one, like two old friends sharing roasted chestnuts. At dawn neither of you is sure who won, and both of you are happy.

events.text: A king of great power, {npc}, whose realm stretches from sea to sea, comes to the gate at night in plain clothes with one guard. "I have enemies at my court," {he} says. "I know who they are. I only need you to point. One lowered head, and the whole realm will believe it."

choices.text: "Point at them yourself, then. You know who they are"

effects.log: {npc} opens {his} mouth and closes it. "I do not know," {he} says at last. "I suspect." "Then you have no enemies," you say, "only suspicions. Go and find out." {He} goes, and does, and finds two, and not the ones {he} suspected.

choices.text: Lower your head at the king

effects.log: {npc}'s guard draws, and then puts the sword away very slowly. The king goes white. You have told {him} who the real enemy at {his} court is: the one who would use a haechi as a weapon. {He} takes it well, eventually.

events.text: An old warrior, {npc}, comes to the gate on two sticks, ninety years old. Seventy years ago, in a great fire, {he} fought the flames beside you on the burning streets with a spear and a wet blanket, and you swallowed what came over {his} head. "I wanted to see you once more," {he} says, "before the fire that takes me, which is a slow one."

choices.text: Lie down beside {him} all afternoon

effects.log: You talk about the fire, which you both remember differently, and then about nothing. At sunset {npc} goes home on {his} two sticks and dies that winter in bed, warm, and is buried with the wet blanket, which {he} kept.

choices.text: Ring the bell, once, for {him}

effects.log: One soft note, the note of that night. {npc} stands very straight on the two sticks and salutes, as soldiers did then. The whole gate salutes back, without knowing why.

events.text: A new governor of the western province, proud of a new horse, rides straight past the stone marker where every official must dismount, and on toward the gate, looking at you over the horse's ears as if to say that a thousand years is long enough for any custom.

choices.text: Stand up

effects.log: The horse stops of its own accord, a long way from you, and refuses to take another step. The governor gets down, red to the ears, and walks the rest of the way, and the whole gate pretends not to have seen.

choices.text: Lie still and look at the horse, not the rider

effects.log: The horse, which is honest, as horses are, lowers its head to you. The governor, perched on a bowing horse in front of the entire court, finds there is nothing to do but get down.

choices.text: Let it go. Custom is not law

effects.log: He rides through. Nobody follows his example, which is the custom's way of answering. He is known for the rest of his career as the governor who rode past the haechi, and he never quite understands why that is not a compliment.

events.text: A small prince of six, on a pony, comes up the road behind the officials, and at the stone marker climbs down very carefully, because his tutor told him to, and walks up to you, and bows, and says: "Is it true you know when people are lying?" The officials behind him hold their breath.

choices.text: "Yes"

effects.log: He thinks about it with great seriousness. "Then I will not lie to you," he says, "ever." He is king forty years later, and he keeps it, which is rarer in kings than you would hope.

choices.text: "Sometimes. Not always. Nobody always does"

effects.log: He looks disappointed, then relieved. "Me neither," he confides. His tutor, who was very nervous, writes down the whole exchange that night, and it is copied out by royal tutors for three hundred years.

events.text: An old official, quite blind, is led up the road by a servant, and gets down from his horse at the wrong place, twenty paces short of the marker, and walks the rest. The young officials behind him laugh. The servant says, quietly, that the old official has done it on purpose every morning for forty years: he gets down where he first saw you, when he was a clerk, and could still see.

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to him

effects.log: The young officials stop laughing. The old official cannot see the bow. The servant tells him, and he stands very still in the road for a moment, and then goes in to the audience, and that morning, everyone says, argues better than he has in years.

choices.text: Lower your head at the young officials who laughed

effects.log: Six young officials find themselves walking backwards to the stone marker, and then twenty paces further, and getting down there too, every morning, for a month. Some of them keep doing it for the rest of their lives, without being able to say why.

events.text: An envoy from beyond the sea, in strange clothes, stops at the marker and asks the interpreter why everyone gets down here. The interpreter, who is in a hurry, says it is because the haechi bites. That is not true. You have never bitten anyone at the dismount line in all your years.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The haechi bites. Yawn, so the envoy sees your teeth are only teeth

effects.log: You yawn, hugely and slowly. The envoy laughs. The interpreter, embarrassed, explains properly: here is where the palace begins, and here is where the beast that sees lies down, and people walk the rest of the way because walking makes you think. The envoy writes this down, and it is the only thing about the capital the envoy's country ever gets right.

choices.text: Lie still. It is a good story, and it keeps the road clear

effects.log: The envoy gets down very quickly and walks past you on the far side of the road. The story goes home across the sea, and for a hundred years the haechi of the capital is drawn in that country with enormous teeth.

events.text: Two village guardian posts, carved poles with fierce painted faces, the Great General of Heaven and the Female General of the Underworld, have pulled themselves out of the ground at the entrance to their village and walked all the way to the capital to accuse each other. A smallpox spirit got into the village last winter. Each says the other was supposed to be watching the road.

choices.text: Ask the village which way the spirit came

effects.log: It came by the river, not the road, where neither post was standing. Neither of them failed. You send them home, both, and suggest a third post by the river. The village carves one that spring, a small one with an anxious face.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The Female General was asleep. Say so to the Great General

effects.log: The Great General was lying about her, out of embarrassment: he had been watching the road, the wrong way. Neither failed on purpose. They walk home together, arguing, and stand at the village entrance arguing for another hundred years, which is how the village likes them.

choices.text: Lower your head at the Great General of Heaven

effects.log: The great painted pole goes home in disgrace and is pulled down and burned by the village elders. The next winter the spirit comes by the river again. Something in your horn cracks.

events.text: A spark in the dye-works by the canal, where the indigo vats stand in long sheds and the dried safflower is stacked in bales to the roof. Red smoke, then blue, then a column of every colour the city wears, going straight up into a windless sky. The dye-masters are running toward it with nothing in their hands.

choices.text: Swallow it, colour by colour

effects.log: Safflower fire tastes red, indigo fire tastes of the sea. You swallow all of it, and for a year your breath comes out in faint colours, and children follow you to watch. (-20 health)

choices.text: Ring the bell and push the vats over onto the flames

ok.log: Forty vats of indigo go over in a blue flood. The fire goes out with a hiss you can hear in the palace. The canal runs blue for a week.

fail.log: The vats are too heavy and the bales too dry. The dye-works go, and the cloth market beside them, and the streets beyond. A quarter of the city. (A great fire)

events.text: A sect of great power invites you to its founding anniversary in the hills, and lays before you, on a table of red lacquer, the gift of a clean spring: its own sacred spring, the clearest in three provinces, to drink from whenever you like. All it asks in return is one quiet year. Its elders have a case coming before the censors.

choices.text: Drink from the spring once, and say no

effects.log: It is very clean water. You drink, and thank them, and lower your head at the elder who keeps the sect's second ledger. The anniversary feast ends early.

choices.text: Ask the elders why a clean spring needs a quiet year

effects.log: Nobody answers. Nobody needs to. The case before the censors goes as it should, and the sect, to its credit, leaves the spring open to you anyway, out of embarrassment.

choices.text: Accept the spring

effects.log: A spring for a year. The water is clean. The year is quiet. The horn, which was washed in the spring all year, is somehow dirtier at the end of it than at the start.

events.text: A sect alchemist has worked out that if a haechi cannot be caught, it can be poisoned: honey cakes, very sweet, laced with a sleeping powder, left at the gate in the name of a grateful widow. They smell of honey, and of something under the honey, and of a widow who does not exist.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The widow is grateful. Leave the cakes and follow the smell home

effects.log: The smell under the honey leads you down four lanes to an alchemist's back room with the rest of the batch on a tray. The censors take it from there.

choices.text: Leave the cakes for the gatekeeper to throw away

effects.log: The gatekeeper throws them in the canal. Three carp sleep for a week. The alchemist tries again the next year, with persimmons.

choices.text: Eat one, to be polite

effects.log: You sleep for three days before the gate with your horn on the paving. Men with a saw are halfway across the square when the gatekeeper's dog wakes you. (-15 health)

events.text: A very old human of great cultivation, {npc}, comes to the gate and sits down. "My grandmother's grandmother," {he} says, "told one small lie at a spring, young, and then confessed it, out loud, before a beast with one horn came out of the mist. And the beast bowed. The family has told it for three hundred years. I wanted to see if it was true."

choices.text: Lay your ears back and bow to {him}, the same way

effects.log: {npc} laughs, and then, unexpectedly, weeps. "It was true," {he} says. "All of it. I always thought the bow was added later." You remember the spring, and the mist, and a witness who said "I did not look" in a loud clear voice.

choices.text: Tell {him} what the lie was

effects.log: "The lie was about a boundary stone that was never looked at," you say. "For a friend." {npc} shakes {his} head, smiling. "That is not how the family tells it. In our version it was much braver." "The true one was braver," you say. "It was taken back, out loud."

events.text: A censor of the Inspector-General's office comes to the gate at night, {npc}, very old, in a hat with your face on it. "I sat my first night tea with a junior who wrote the clerk's name on the board, all those years ago," {he} says, "before the stone beast moved. That junior is dead now. I am the last one who saw it. I wanted to tell you we did it right, most of the time, after that."

choices.text: "I know. I watched"

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. "Most of the time," {he} says again, honestly. "Not always." "Nobody always does," you say, and {he} laughs, and pours two cups of tea that have gone quite cold, as they always did.

choices.text: Ask about the times you did not

effects.log: {npc} tells you, all night, every board that went up wrong and every one that should have and did not. It is a long list, and an honest one. In the morning {he} goes home lighter, and you lie before the gate a little heavier, which is how a confession should go.

events.text: A door you have never felt before: a painting of you on the wall of a court in heaven itself, painted by an immortal who once saw you lie before a gate below. Through it you can hear a case: a minor god of a crossroads, accused of misdirecting travellers into a bandits' pass. The god swears it pointed true.

choices.text: (the horn: a lie) The god pointed true. Step out of the heavenly wall and lower your head

effects.log: The crossroads god was paid in roasted chestnuts by the bandits, a sack a year. The court of heaven, which has never had a beast step out of its walls before, is extremely impressed, and somewhat alarmed.

choices.text: Ask the travellers who came back

effects.log: Three travellers who escaped the pass are found and asked. All three were sent left by the god, toward the pass, with a smile. The crossroads god is moved to a crossroads with only one road.

choices.text: Stay in the paint. Heaven has its own judges

effects.log: The god is acquitted. The pass goes on taking travellers. You hear about each one, through the paint, and remember that you could have stepped out.
